AML-01.title: Money Laundering (Placement, Layering, Integration)
AML-01.one_screen: Criminals attempt to disguise illicit proceeds by processing funds through multiple steps (often called placement, layering, integration) to make them appear legitimate. In practice these steps can overlap or repeat rather than being strictly sequential.

sources.label: FinCEN, *Money Laundering and the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA)* (US Treasury, Feb 2022).
PMLA 2002 (India), Section 3 definition of ML (via FIU-IND site).

AML-02.title: Terrorist Financing
AML-02.one_screen: Terrorist financing is collecting or providing funds to support terrorism. Unlike money laundering, it may involve funds from lawful sources and focuses on concealing the destination and purpose of money, not necessarily its origin.

sources.label: Egmont Group, *Basel AML Handbook (CFT Section)*.
FATF Guidance on Terrorist Financing (risk indicators).

AML-03.title: Proliferation Financing
AML-03.one_screen: Proliferation financing is the provision of funds or financial services for the creation or spread of weapons of mass destruction. It is illegal under UN sanctions and FATF standards, and financial institutions must screen against WMD sanctions lists.

sources.label: Gibraltar FIAU, *Anti-Money Laundering & Countering Terrorist Financing Guidance* (defining PF in line with FATF/UN).
FATF, *Guidance on Counter Proliferation Financing* (2022).

AML-04.title: FATF and Global Standards
AML-04.one_screen: The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) is an international body that sets AML/CFT standards (40+9 Recommendations). Its rules aren’t laws, but countries adopt them locally. FATF conducts mutual evaluations and classifies jurisdictions into “grey” (monitored) and “black” (high-risk) lists.

sources.label: FATF, *The FATF Recommendations (updated 2023)*.
FATF, *High-Risk Jurisdictions - Call for Action (black list) and Increased Monitoring (grey list)* (June 2026).

AML-05.title: Banks as AML Gatekeepers
AML-05.one_screen: Banks act as the financial system’s “first line of defense.” They are legally required to verify customers (KYC), monitor transactions, and report suspicious activity. Regulators rely on banks to enforce AML rules because banks handle the cash flows criminals need.

sources.label: RBI, *Master Direction – Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction* (2025) (outlining banks’ AML duties).
FinCEN, *BSA Compliance (e.g., CIP Rule 31 CFR 1020.220)* (discussing banks’ gatekeeper role in preventing criminal money entering the system).

AML-06.title: KYC and Customer Identification (CIP)
AML-06.one_screen: “Know Your Customer” (KYC) is the process of verifying a customer’s identity before opening an account. In the US this is called the Customer Identification Program (CIP). Banks must collect official ID, confirm it is valid, and record it.

sources.label: RBI, *Master Direction – Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction* (2025).
FFIEC BSA/AML Manual (US CIP Rule).

AML-07.title: Beneficial Ownership
AML-07.one_screen: Beneficial owner (BO) means the natural person(s) who ultimately owns or controls a customer (especially a company), even if not listed on official records. Laws typically use ownership thresholds (e.g. >10% in India, >25% in US) to identify BOs.

sources.label: RBI, *Master Direction – Know Your Customer (KYC)* (2025).
FinCEN FAQ on *Beneficial Ownership Information Reporting*.

AML-08.title: Politically Exposed Persons (PEPs)
AML-08.one_screen: A PEP is someone entrusted with a prominent public function (e.g. senior politician, military officer). Because of corruption risk, PEPs (and their family/close associates) require enhanced due diligence.

sources.label: FATF, *Guidance on Politically Exposed Persons (2013)*.
FinCEN, *Advisory (Nov 2020) on PEP definition*.

AML-09.title: Risk-Based Approach (RBA)
AML-09.one_screen: The risk-based approach means allocating AML resources according to the risk posed by each customer or transaction. Banks must assess risk factors (customer type, geography, product) and adjust due diligence intensity accordingly.

sources.label: FATF, *Guidance on the Risk-Based Approach to AML* (e.g. FATF Rec. 1).
Basel Committee, *Customer Risk Factors (CBB 2021)* (summary of RBA concepts).

AML-10.title: Simplified vs Enhanced Due Diligence (SDD vs EDD)
AML-10.one_screen: Due diligence intensity is matched to risk. Enhanced Due Diligence (EDD) means extra checks (for high-risk clients, e.g. PEPs, high-risk countries). Simplified Due Diligence (SDD) allows reduced checks for very low-risk customers.

sources.label: RBI, *Master Direction – Know Your Customer (KYC)* (2025) (EDD on high-risk countries).
FATF, *AML Risk Factors and EDD Guidance* (Rec. 10/12).

AML-11.title: Ongoing Due Diligence and Periodic Review
AML-11.one_screen: Ongoing due diligence means continuously monitoring a customer and updating their profile as circumstances change. Periodic reviews (refreshing KYC at set intervals) must be done in line with risk level. Regulators expect banks to treat KYC as a “living” process, not a one-time task.

sources.label: FATF Recommendation 10 guidance: firms must conduct ongoing due diligence and periodic review.
Fraxtional (AML blog), *Ongoing Monitoring & Perpetual KYC*.

AML-12.title: Perpetual KYC (Continuous Updating)
AML-12.one_screen: Perpetual KYC is the practice of continuously updating customer profiles rather than relying solely on periodic refreshes. It means automatically re-verifying identity, sanctions, and risk as soon as new data appears (via screening and open sources).

sources.label: Fraxtional (AML blog), *Understanding Ongoing Monitoring & Perpetual KYC*.
ACAMS, *Perpetual KYC concept in AML compliance*.

AML-13.title: Transaction Monitoring
AML-13.one_screen: Transaction monitoring is the automated process of screening payments and account activity for unusual patterns (based on rules, thresholds and typologies). It compares transactions against customer profiles and known risk indicators.

sources.label: Fraxtional (AML blog), *Key Components of Transaction Monitoring*.
ACAMS, *AML Transaction Monitoring Best Practices* (industry typologies summary).

AML-14.title: False Positives and Alert Triage
AML-14.one_screen: Modern AML monitoring flags far more legitimate transactions than criminal ones. Industry data show ~90–95% of alerts are false positives. The challenge is efficiently triaging each alert (reviewing context) to determine if it truly indicates suspicious activity.

sources.label: FluxForce (AML analytics) *What percentage of AML alerts are false positives?*.
LexisNexis Risk Solutions, *True Cost of Financial Crime* report (2009) – note on compliance costs and SARs.

AML-15.title: Suspicious Activity Reporting and Tipping Off
AML-15.one_screen: Suspicious activity reports (SARs/STRs) are formal filings to authorities when a financial institution suspects money laundering or terrorist financing. The naming and exact process vary by country (e.g. SAR in US/UK, STR in India). Tipping off (informing the client they’re being reported) is strictly prohibited.

sources.label: UK NCA, *Suspicious Activity Reports Guidance*.
FIU-IND FAQs (on STR filing and tipping-off).

AML-16.title: Sanctions Screening
AML-16.one_screen: Sanctions screening involves checking customer names and transactions against global watchlists (UN, OFAC, etc.). This uses name-matching algorithms (often fuzzy matching) to catch known terrorists, criminals, or sanctioned entities. Screening is distinct from transaction monitoring because it matches specific identities rather than patterns.

sources.label: OFAC, *Sanctions List Search Manual* (US Treasury guidance on name screening).
FATF, *Guidance on Compliance with WMD Sanctions* (sanctions screening best practices).

AML-17.title: Fraud and its Relationship to AML
AML-17.one_screen: Fraud involves criminal deception for financial gain, whereas AML deals with concealing illicit funds. They overlap (e.g. fraud proceeds need laundering) and banks increasingly combine fraud and AML monitoring. Key terms: first-party vs third-party fraud, application fraud, mule accounts.

sources.label: GBG, *Application Fraud and First-Party Fraud* (explains first-party vs third-party).
Flagright, *Uncovering Money Mules in ML* (industry perspective).

AML-18.title: AML Governance and Oversight
AML-18.one_screen: Governance sets up the AML framework: a designated compliance officer (MLRO/Principal Officer) ensures policy, training and reporting. Transaction monitoring and screening models count as regulated models subject to validation (MRM principles). Regulators typically enforce AML by penalizing failures (e.g. missing STRs, inadequate controls).

sources.label: RBI, *Master Direction – KYC & AML* (appointment of Principal Officer and obligations).
UK NCA, *Proceeds of Crime Act* (offences for failure to report).
FinCEN/OFAC enforcement press releases (on AML fines).

BA-01.title: Role of the Business Analyst (vs Product/Project Manager)
BA-01.one_screen: A BA in a bank translates business needs into requirements, focusing on *what* and *why*, unlike a product manager (who defines product strategy and features) or a project manager (who plans the *how* and *when* of delivery).

sources.label: Harvard Business Review (via Medium) – role distinctions
ICS Learn – BA vs PM (“what/why” vs “how/when”)

BA-02.title: Change Landscape: Regulatory vs Strategic vs Remediation
BA-02.one_screen: Banks undertake strategic initiatives (growth or efficiency) and remediation (fixing defects), but *regulatory-driven* change is mandatory, with fixed deadlines and external oversight, requiring full compliance and auditability.

sources.label: Walper & Winter (ISACA Journal) – regulatory change maturity (Audit trails, exam readiness)
Ramki Ravulapalli – “Regulatory Projects” (waterfall, deadlines)

BA-03.title: Stakeholders in Bank Change Programs
BA-03.one_screen: Successful change requires early and ongoing involvement of all impacted groups: business owners (front-line and process managers), risk and compliance, finance, IT/operations, data/model owners, internal audit and (where needed) the regulator.

sources.label: Yethi Consulting – Core banking UAT participants and coverage
RiskSpan – model owner vs validator roles and documentation

BA-04.title: Requirements Elicitation Techniques
BA-04.one_screen: Elicitation is gathering information on what stakeholders need.  Techniques include structured interviews, workshops, observation, document analysis, surveys, and prototyping, chosen based on context and participant availability.

sources.label: Bridging the Gap – “5 Best Requirement Elicitation Techniques” (interviews, observation, etc.)
Bridging the Gap – Eliciting from Busy Stakeholders (importance of agenda, homework)

BA-05.title: Interviewing Time-Pressed Subject Matter Experts
BA-05.one_screen: SMEs are often busy and short on time.  Always prepare an agenda and pre-reads, ask targeted questions, and build credibility so even a short meeting is productive.

sources.label: Bridging the Gap – “Interviewing a Subject Matter Expert” (be prepared, agenda)

BA-06.title: Process Mapping (As-Is vs To-Be)
BA-06.one_screen: Process mapping diagrams the workflow of a process.  Mapping the current “as-is” process clarifies existing steps and bottlenecks; the “to-be” map lays out the improved future workflow.  Visualizing both highlights where changes are needed.

sources.label: IBM Blueprint (IBM KB) – “A process map outlines steps... reveals areas of improvement”
IBM – definition of process mapping for clarity

BA-07.title: Root Cause Analysis
BA-07.one_screen: Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is a method to find the underlying cause of a problem or error, not just its symptoms.  Techniques like “5 Whys” and fishbone diagrams are used to dig down to the true source of an issue.

sources.label: BA Times – “Root Cause Analysis is a method of identifying the underlying cause of a problem... using cause-and-effect diagrams, flowcharts, etc.”

BA-08.title: Requirements Traceability (Matrix)
BA-08.one_screen: A traceability matrix links each requirement through design, code and testing.  It ensures every requirement (especially regulatory ones) is accounted for and verified.  This audit trail of requirements-to-tests is vital for regulators and audits.

sources.label: Visure Solutions – “Traceability Matrix... traces and maps requirements to project artifacts... gives a clear audit trail to demonstrate compliance”

BA-09.title: Business Requirements Document (BRD)
BA-09.one_screen: The BRD captures *what* the business wants and *why*, including objectives, scope, stakeholders, and high-level requirements. It **must not** include solution design or technical details. Each requirement should have acceptance criteria.

sources.label: Monday.com – capturing requirements with acceptance criteria

BA-10.title: Functional Specifications vs Business Requirements
BA-10.one_screen: **Business requirements** state *what* is needed, while **functional specifications** describe *how* the system will meet those needs.  A business requirement is high-level (e.g. “produce regulatory report X”), whereas a functional spec details the software logic, screens, or data elements to implement it. The BRD avoids technical detail.

sources.label: Monday.com – “no excessive technical detail” in BRD template

BA-11.title: Data Mapping Specification
BA-11.one_screen: A data mapping spec is a field-by-field table linking each source field to a target field, including data type and the transformation rule.  It documents exactly how data moves or is converted from the old system to the new.

sources.label: BA Careers – Definition of data mapping and example mapping table

BA-12.title: Non-Functional Requirements (Performance, Retention, Auditability)
BA-12.one_screen: Non-functional requirements define *how* the system performs: its quality attributes like speed, security, data retention, and audit capabilities. In banking, **auditability** (e.g. full logging and data retention) is often mandated for compliance.

sources.label: LinkedIn (Rosmary Okordion) – banking NFRs including Auditability requirement

BA-13.title: Testable Acceptance Criteria
BA-13.one_screen: Acceptance criteria are the specific, testable conditions that define when a requirement is met.  Well-crafted criteria are clear, concise, and objectively verifiable.

sources.label: Atlassian – “Acceptance criteria are... testable statements”
Atlassian – acceptance criteria must be “objectively verifiable”

BA-14.title: User Stories and Acceptance in a Regulated Context
BA-14.one_screen: In agile development, user stories (“As a user, I want…”) drive increments.  In a regulated project, each story’s acceptance criteria must tie back to formal requirements and evidence.  You may still use stories, but supplement them with thorough documentation and approvals for audit purposes.

sources.label: Atlassian – importance of acceptance criteria as requirements verification (contextual)
Industry best practice – agile in banking still requires traceability and approvals. (No specific cite)

BA-15.title: Testing Lifecycle (Unit, System, Integration, UAT)
BA-15.one_screen: A typical banking IT change goes through multiple test phases: Unit testing (by developers), Integration/System testing (by QA/IT), and User Acceptance Testing (by business).  Each phase has different owners and objectives.

sources.label: Yethi Consulting – Core banking UAT (business-led)

BA-16.title: Test Planning and Test Packs
BA-16.one_screen: A test plan defines the scope, approach, resources, and schedule of testing. Test packs (test cases and data) list the specific scenarios with expected outcomes.  For each requirement, predefined test cases and datasets must be prepared before testing begins.

sources.label: OCM Solution – outlines cutover/go-live steps (implied planning)

BA-17.title: UAT Coverage and Defect Management
BA-17.one_screen: Ensure UAT covers all critical business and regulatory scenarios. Use metrics (e.g. scenario coverage %) to argue sufficiency.  Manage defects by classifying each by *severity* (technical impact) and *priority* (business urgency).

sources.label: Yethi Consulting – Core banking UAT includes metrics like scenario coverage
GeeksforGeeks – severity vs priority definitions

BA-18.title: Parallel Running & Go-Live Planning
BA-18.one_screen: *Parallel running* means operating the old and new systems side-by-side for a period to compare outputs. *Go-live planning* (cutover) details how to switch to the new system, including rollback steps if needed.  Both are critical in regulated transitions.

sources.label: OCM Solution – “Cutover and rollback steps” in go-live checklist

BA-19.title: Post-Implementation Review and Benefits Realisation
BA-19.one_screen: After go-live, conduct a formal review comparing actual outcomes to planned objectives. Capture lessons learned and track whether expected benefits (cost savings, efficiency gains, compliance) are realized.

sources.label: Project Delivery (UK government) – benefits management and review principles (general reference)

BA-20.title: Waterfall vs Agile in Banking
BA-20.one_screen: Waterfall (stage-gate) and Agile (iterative) are both used in banks.  Regulatory changes often lean waterfall: fixed scope and deadlines drive sequential phases (requirements→design→build→test). Agile is better for evolving requirements, but must be adapted for compliance needs.

sources.label: Ramki Ravulapalli – “Banks deal with regulatory initiatives by setting up Waterfall style... finalise requirements, then design, then build and test”

BA-21.title: Prioritisation & Estimation in Banking Projects
BA-21.one_screen: Prioritize work using clear criteria (business value, risk, regulatory urgency) and defend choices with data.  Estimate tasks realistically using ranges or past data, accounting for optimism bias.

sources.label: Planning fallacy (behavioral economics) – people underestimate tasks

BA-22.title: Managing Scope Change with Fixed Deadlines
BA-22.one_screen: In projects with immovable regulatory deadlines, handle scope changes through a formal change control process.  Assess each new requirement’s impact on timeline and scope. If the deadline cannot move, negotiate resources or de-scope non-critical items rather than slipping the date.

sources.label: Monday.com – formal change request process with impact assessment

CAP-01.title: Why Regulatory Capital Exists
CAP-01.one_screen: Expected loss is the recurring, statistically anticipated cost of taking risk; unexpected loss is the adverse tail beyond that expectation. Provisions and pricing address expected loss, while capital exists principally to keep the bank solvent when realised losses exceed what was expected.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Modifications to the capital treatment for expected and unexpected credit losses*, BCBS 104, 30 January 2004
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE30 — IRB approach: overview and asset class definitions*
Bank for International Settlements, *Forecasting expected and unexpected losses*, Working Papers No 913, 2020

CAP-02.title: Solvency and Liquidity in a Capital Context
CAP-02.one_screen: Solvency asks whether the value of the bank’s assets can absorb losses and still cover its liabilities; liquidity asks whether cash obligations can be met when due. Capital protects solvency, while liquidity resources protect payment capacity, and a bank can fail either test without initially failing the other.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework*, capital and liquidity standards
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*

CAP-03.title: Going-Concern and Gone-Concern Capital
CAP-03.one_screen: Going-concern capital absorbs losses while the bank remains operating; gone-concern capital protects creditors and supports resolution once viability has been lost. Basel places CET1 and AT1 in Tier 1 going-concern capital and characterises Tier 2 as gone-concern capital.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*
Bank for International Settlements Financial Stability Institute, *Strengthening the going-concern role of AT1: options and trade-offs*, FSI Briefs No 32, 11 June 2026

CAP-04.title: The Regulatory Capital Stack
CAP-04.one_screen: Regulatory capital is a quality hierarchy: CET1 is the first and strongest loss absorber, AT1 supplements going-concern capital, and Tier 2 provides lower-ranking gone-concern capacity. Basel total regulatory capital is CET1 plus AT1 plus Tier 2, after applicable regulatory adjustments.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*

CAP-05.title: Regulatory Adjustments and Deductions
CAP-05.one_screen: Accounting equity is not automatically regulatory capital. Prudential deductions and adjustments remove or limit balance-sheet items whose value may be unavailable, uncertain or double-counted precisely when the bank needs loss-absorbing capital most.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP30 — Regulatory adjustments*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CAP10 — Definition of eligible capital*

CAP-06.title: The Capital Buffer Stack
CAP-06.one_screen: Minimum capital is the line a bank must not normally cross; buffers are deliberately placed above that line so capital can absorb stress before minimum requirements are breached. Conservation, countercyclical and systemic buffers serve different purposes even when all are expressed as additional CET1 requirements.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC30 — Buffers above the regulatory minimum*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025*, 28 November 2025
Federal Reserve Board, *Supervision and Regulation*, 2023 Annual Report

CAP-07.title: Distribution Constraints and Maximum Distributable Amount
CAP-07.one_screen: Buffers bite before minimums because entering the buffer restricts distributions while the bank can still remain legally capitalised above minimum requirements. The maximum distributable amount mechanism turns buffer depletion into progressively stronger limits on dividends, variable remuneration and other discretionary payouts.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *The capital buffers in Basel III — Executive Summary*, 28 November 2019
Prudential Regulation Authority, *CP9/24 — Streamlining the Pillar 2A capital framework and the capital communications process*, 12 September 2024
European Banking Authority, *EBA calls for more certainty and consistency in the application of restrictions on distributions*, 18 December 2015

CAP-08.title: The Leverage Ratio Backstop
CAP-08.one_screen: The leverage ratio ignores most risk weights and compares Tier 1 capital with a broad exposure measure. It is a deliberately blunt backstop: risk-based models can change the measured riskiness of assets, but they cannot make the underlying exposure disappear.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, LEV20 — Calculation of the leverage ratio*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy Directions, 2025*, para 262, 28 November 2025
Bank of England, *Financial Stability in Focus: The FPC's assessment of bank capital requirements*, 2 December 2025

CAP-09.title: Risk Weights and Risk-Weighted Assets
CAP-09.one_screen: A risk weight converts an exposure amount into a regulatory risk measure: exposure × risk weight = RWA under the basic standardised credit-risk logic. The weight is a prudential calibration of relative risk, not a forecast that the stated percentage of the exposure will be lost.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE20 — Standardised approach: individual exposures*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*

CAP-10.title: Basel’s Three Pillars
CAP-10.one_screen: Pillar 1 supplies minimum quantitative capital rules, Pillar 2 adds bank-specific risk assessment and supervisory review, and Pillar 3 uses public disclosure to strengthen market discipline. A complete capital framework therefore asks not only “what does the formula require?” but also “what risks did the formula miss?” and “what must outsiders be told?”

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework*, supervisory review and disclosure modules
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, SRP20 — Four key principles of supervisory review*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, DIS10 — Scope and application of Pillar 3*

CAP-11.title: The Four RWA Components
CAP-11.one_screen: Total RWA aggregates distinct prudential risk engines: credit risk, market risk, operational risk and credit valuation adjustment risk. They share the same capital denominator only after each component has been measured under its own rules.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, MAR50 — Credit valuation adjustment framework*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, OPE25 — Standardised approach*

CAP-12.title: The Standardised Approach to Credit Risk
CAP-12.one_screen: Under the standardised approach, the regulator prescribes the exposure classes, eligibility conditions and risk-weight rules instead of allowing the bank to generate the core credit-risk capital requirement from its own PD/LGD models. Revised Basel rules make this approach more granular and risk-sensitive while retaining external ratings only where the framework permits them.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE20 — Standardised approach: individual exposures*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397, 27 April 2026
Prudential Regulation Authority, *PS1/26 — Implementation of Basel 3.1: Final rules*, 20 January 2026

CAP-13.title: Foundation and Advanced IRB
CAP-13.one_screen: IRB allows approved banks to use internal estimates for specified credit-risk parameters, but the bank never owns the whole capital formula. Under Foundation IRB the supervisor supplies more of the loss parameters; under Advanced IRB the bank estimates more of them, subject to permission, constraints and validation.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE31 — IRB approach: risk-weight functions*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE32 — IRB approach: risk components*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397

CAP-14.title: The IRB Risk-Weight Function
CAP-14.one_screen: The IRB function turns PD, LGD, EAD and maturity into a capital measure while applying a supervisory correlation structure. Higher default likelihood, larger loss severity, larger exposure or longer effective maturity generally increase capital, but the function is nonlinear because it is designed around adverse portfolio loss rather than a simple PD × LGD calculation.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE31 — IRB approach: risk-weight functions*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE32 — IRB approach: risk components*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE30 — IRB approach: overview and asset class definitions*

CAP-15.title: IRB Input Floors and Parameter Constraints
CAP-15.one_screen: Input floors stop internally estimated risk parameters from falling below prudential lower bounds even when a model produces a smaller number. They constrain the ingredients of the IRB calculation; the output floor constrains the final aggregate RWA result.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE32 — IRB approach: risk components*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397

CAP-16.title: The Output Floor
CAP-16.one_screen: The output floor prevents approved internal models from reducing total RWA below 72.5% of the amount produced by the prescribed standardised comparison at full implementation. It is an aggregate backstop against model risk and excessive RWA variability, not a rule that replaces internal models with a 72.5% risk weight.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, RBC20 — Calculation of minimum risk-based capital requirements*
Prudential Regulation Authority, *PS9/24 — Implementation of the Basel 3.1 standards: near-final policy statement, Part 2*, 12 September 2024
European Commission, *Commission Staff Working Document, SWD(2026) 615*, output-floor implementation table

CAP-17.title: Specialised Lending and Supervisory Slotting
CAP-17.one_screen: Slotting converts a specialised-lending exposure into a supervisory quality category and assigns the corresponding regulatory treatment rather than relying on an ordinary corporate PD/LGD model. It is designed for financing whose repayment depends materially on the performance of a specific asset, project or cash-flow structure.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE33 — IRB approach: supervisory slotting approach for specialised lending*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397

CAP-18.title: Credit Risk Mitigation: Collateral, Guarantees and Netting
CAP-18.one_screen: Credit risk mitigation reduces regulatory exposure only when the protection is eligible, legally effective and recognised by the applicable capital rules. Collateral changes the loss available from pledged assets, guarantees transfer specified credit risk to a protection provider, and netting reduces exposure by recognising enforceable offsetting claims.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE22 — Standardised approach: credit risk mitigation*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, Chapter V, RBI/DOR/2026-27/397

CAP-19.title: Substitution and Comprehensive CRM Approaches
CAP-19.one_screen: Substitution changes whose credit quality drives the protected portion of an exposure; the comprehensive collateral approach changes the exposure value after recognising collateral and prescribed valuation adjustments. One changes the relevant risk weight, the other changes the amount to which risk weighting is applied.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE22 — Standardised approach: credit risk mitigation*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, Chapter V

CAP-20.title: Haircuts
CAP-20.one_screen: A haircut is a prudential valuation adjustment that recognises that exposure and collateral values can move before a position is closed or collateral is realised. It deliberately prevents yesterday’s collateral market value from being treated as perfectly certain protection against tomorrow’s exposure.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, CRE22 — Standardised approach: credit risk mitigation*
Reserve Bank of India, *Commercial Banks – Capital Charge for Credit Risk – Standardised Approach Directions, 2026*, supervisory haircut provisions

CAP-21.title: Pillar 1 and Pillar 2
CAP-21.one_screen: Pillar 1 standardises minimum capital for risks that can be captured through common formulas; Pillar 2 asks whether those formulas leave material institution-specific risk uncovered. Pillar 2 is therefore the deliberate completeness check on Pillar 1.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, SRP20 — Four key principles of supervisory review*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework*, Supervisory Review Process

CAP-22.title: ICAAP and the Supervisory Review Process
CAP-22.one_screen: ICAAP is the bank’s own disciplined assessment of how much capital it needs for its actual risk profile and strategy; supervisory review tests whether that assessment is credible. It is not a worksheet for reproducing regulatory minima.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, SRP20 — Four key principles of supervisory review*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, SRP30 — Risk management*

CAP-23.title: Stress Testing and Capital Transmission
CAP-23.one_screen: A capital stress test is a causal chain: define an adverse scenario, translate it into risk drivers and financial losses, project earnings and RWA, then recalculate capital resources and ratios. Reverse stress testing runs the chain backwards from failure to identify combinations of events capable of breaking the business model.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Stress testing principles*, 17 October 2018
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework, SRP30 — Risk management*

CAP-24.title: Supervisory and Internal Stress Tests
CAP-24.one_screen: Internal stress tests are management tools tailored to the bank’s own vulnerabilities; supervisory stress tests are authority-led or authority-specified exercises designed to assess prudential resilience and comparability. The same scenario can serve both purposes, but ownership, objectives and consequences are different.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Stress testing principles*, 17 October 2018

Federal Reserve Board, *Federal Reserve Board finalizes hypothetical scenarios for its annual stress test and votes to maintain the current stress test-related capital requirements until public feedback can be considered*, 4 February 2026

CAP-25.title: Basel Does Not Bind Banks Directly
CAP-25.one_screen: Basel is an international prudential standard, not a supranational banking statute. The Basel Committee expressly has no formal supranational authority and its decisions have no legal force; binding obligations arise only when competent jurisdictions implement the standards through their own law and supervisory rulebooks.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Committee Charter*, section 3 “Legal status”, 5 June 2018
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework*

Small Domestic Deposit Takers enter the PRA’s simplified capital regime on **1 January 2027**, creating a deliberately different domestic framework for eligible smaller firms.

CCR-01.title: Counterparty Credit Risk
CCR-01.one_screen: Counterparty credit risk is the risk that a counterparty defaults before final settlement of a transaction, exposing a bank to potential loss. It differs from standard loan credit risk because exposure is contingent on market movements, not a fixed loan balance. Either party can owe a positive amount in derivative trades, making it a bilateral risk.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, “Final guidelines for counterparty credit risk management”, BIS press release (Dec 2024) (BCBS definition of CCR risk).
Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance on Counterparty Credit Risk Management” (2010) (definitions of exposure and wrong-way risk).
Dirk Bullmann, “FX settlement risk and PvP” (CLS Group, 2023) (Herstatt/settlement risk discussion).

CCR-02.title: Current vs Potential Exposure
CCR-02.one_screen: CCR measurement distinguishes between current exposure (replacement cost) and potential future exposure. Current exposure is the positive mark-to-market value of a trade today. Potential future exposure is an estimate of how much the exposure could increase over time due to market movements, reflecting the contract’s uncertainty.

sources.label: Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance on CCR” (2010) (definitions of expected exposure and PFE).
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BCBS 279 (2014) (SA-CCR uses RC + PFE).

CCR-03.title: Exposure Metrics (EE, EPE, Peak)
CCR-03.one_screen: Banks summarize CCR over time using metrics like Expected Exposure (EE), Expected Positive Exposure (EPE), and peak exposure. These metrics aggregate exposure profiles into single numbers for capital and limit setting. EPE is essentially the time-weighted average of expected exposures (only when positive) over the first year; peak exposure is the high percentile of exposures.

sources.label: Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance on CCR” (2010) (definitions of EPE and peak exposure).
BIS/BCBS SA-CCR standard (2014) (general structure using EAD).

CCR-04.title: Wrong-Way Risk
CCR-04.one_screen: Wrong-way risk arises when market movements that increase exposure to a counterparty coincide with an increase in that counterparty’s default probability. In general WWR, the counterparty’s credit quality worsens with adverse market factors. In specific WWR, a direct link exists (e.g. the counterparty has credit exposure to the underlying).

sources.label: Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance on CCR” (2010) (definition of specific and general wrong-way risk).
Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” (2014) (risk-sensitive approach accounts for netting and margin, implicitly addressing WWR concerns).

CCR-05.title: Close-Out Netting
CCR-05.one_screen: Close-out netting is a legal mechanism allowing a bank to terminate all transactions with a defaulted counterparty and net them into a single amount owed by one party to the other. If enforceable, netting greatly reduces exposure, since only the netted positive value is at risk rather than each trade’s full value.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” (2014) (netting recognition in EAD).
Legal analyses of netting (e.g., ISDA whitepapers on enforceability).

CCR-06.title: Collateral and Margin
CCR-06.one_screen: Collateral is a key mitigation tool for CCR. Variation margin (VM) and initial margin (IM) are two collateral types. VM is exchanged to cover current mark-to-market exposure daily, protecting against immediate losses. IM is posted upfront or periodically to cover potential future exposure over a margin period of risk.

sources.label: Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance on CCR” (2010) (high-level risk management).
CME Group, “Uncleared Margin Rules” (2020) (timeline of VM/IM phases).
ISDA publications on collateral.

CCR-07.title: Margin Period of Risk & Related Terms
CCR-07.one_screen: The margin period of risk (MPR) is the time assumed between a counterparty’s default and the liquidation or hedging of the position. It determines how much additional future price movement risk the initial margin must cover. Regulators often assume 10 days or more for the MPR.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” (2014) (assumes margin period in calculations).
ISDA/ industry literature on CSAs and MPR.

CCR-08.title: Rehypothecation
CCR-08.one_screen: Rehypothecation is the practice where the collateral receiver re-uses (re-pledges) the client’s collateral to fund its own activities. This can create risk: if the receiver defaults, the original pledgor might not get full collateral back.

sources.label: Basel Committee, capital rules on collateral recognition.
IOSCO-BCBS “Margin rules” (2015) on segregation (brief mention).

CCR-09.title: Uncleared Margin Rules
CCR-09.one_screen: The global “Uncleared Margin Rules” (UMR) require banks and other dealers to post both variation and initial margin on non-centrally-cleared OTC derivatives. Phased implementation began in 2016, with the last group of counterparties complying by 2022. UMR ensure broad use of VM/IM even for bilateral trades.

sources.label: CME Group, “Navigating Uncleared Margin Rules” (2020) (timeline of UMR).
BCBS-IOSCO margin requirements standards (2015).

CCR-10.title: Central Clearing and CCPs
CCR-10.one_screen: Central counterparties (CCPs) mitigate bilateral CCR by interposing themselves between participants. When two parties clear through a CCP, each party’s counterparty becomes the CCP. The CCP nets trades among all members and manages default risk via margins and a waterfall. CCP clearing removes bilateral credit exposure but introduces new exposures to the CCP itself.

sources.label: BIS “Capital requirements for bank exposures to central counterparties” (Basel Framework CRE 5.4).
CCIL (India), “Derivatives Settlement” FAQs (explaining CCP for IRS).

CCR-11.title: Default Waterfall
CCR-11.one_screen: A CCP’s default waterfall is its ordered pool of resources to cover a member’s losses. Typically, waterfall layers are: the defaulting member’s initial margin → the member’s default fund contribution → the CCP’s own capital (“skin in the game”) → the mutualized default fund of surviving members. If losses exceed all, additional measures (like assessments or equity auction) are used.

sources.label: CCP rulebooks (e.g. CME, LCH) on default management.
BIS/CPMI-IOSCO guidelines on CCP resilience (2012).

CCR-12.title: Client Clearing Structures
CCR-12.one_screen: When clients clear through a clearing member, there are typically two models: omnibus and segregated. In omnibus clearing, all client positions are pooled under the member’s account; the member’s risk to the CCP is net of all its clients. In segregated clearing, each client’s positions are separately collateralized, isolating them in case the member defaults.

sources.label: BIS/CPMI-IOSCO Principles for financial market infrastructures (client clearing guidelines).
LCH, CME clearing rulebooks (public summaries).

CCR-13.title: CCP Exposures and Capital Treatment
CCR-13.one_screen: Even with clearing, banks must hold capital for exposures to CCPs. Under Basel rules, a clearing member’s trade exposure to a qualifying CCP generally gets a low risk weight (often 2%) reflecting the CCP’s risk-absorbing structure. Client exposures to a CCP (via a member) also have regulatory treatment recognizing default fund offsets.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “Capital requirements for exposures to CCPs” (Basel framework CRE 5.4).
BIS/BCBS QIS reports on CCP (2012).

CCR-14.title: SA-CCR (Standardized Approach to CCR)
CCR-14.one_screen: SA-CCR is the Basel III capital approach for measuring CCR exposure. It computes Exposure at Default (EAD) as **EAD = α × (Replacement Cost + Potential Future Exposure)**, with α=1.4. Replacement Cost (RC) is the positive current value net of haircut collateral. Potential Future Exposure (PFE) is derived from standardized add-on factors by asset class, aggregated by hedging sets and offset by correlation, then net of initial margin (subject to a small 5% floor). This approach accounts for margining, netting, asset classes, and uses a higher multiplier for safety.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” (BCBS 279, 2014) (formal definition of EAD components).
Wikipedia “Standardized approach (CCR)” (summary of formula with α=1.4).
US Fed press release (Nov 2019) (mentions SA-CCR adoption timeline).

CCR-15.title: Internal Model Method (IMM)
CCR-15.one_screen: The Internal Model Method (IMM) allows a bank to use its own approved models to compute CCR exposures (particularly PFE) for capital, subject to strict regulatory criteria. It is most often used for calculating CVA capital under Basel. For exposure, IMM required sophisticated simulation of netting sets and collateral to estimate expected and unexpected exposures. Basel has largely phased out the IMM shortcut (except for CVA) in favor of SA-CCR, but some large banks use IMM for advanced CCR metrics.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” FAQs (notes elimination of IMM shortcut).
Basel III final standards (2017) on CVA.

CCR-16.title: CEM and SM Retirement
CCR-16.one_screen: The old methods for CCR, the Current Exposure Method (CEM) and the Standardized Method (SM), have been replaced by SA-CCR. CEM (used since Basel II) computed CCR as RC + add-on factors on notional by asset class and maturity. SM was a simpler approach for certain transactions. Both were considered insufficiently risk-sensitive. Basel finalized SA-CCR to replace these from 2017 onward.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “SA-CCR” (2014) (explicit replacement of CEM and SM).
Industry analyses of CCR methods (2017).

CCR-17.title: Default vs CVA Capital
CCR-17.one_screen: Basel requires two separate capital charges for counterparty risk: a **default risk charge** (credit risk capital) and a **CVA risk charge**. The default charge covers expected loss if the counterparty outright defaults; CVA capital covers volatility in mark-to-market credit spreads (the risk of the counterparty’s changing credit quality).

sources.label: Basel Committee, “Credit Valuation Adjustment framework” (Basel III final amendments).
US Fed/OCC proposals on CVA (2022) (context).

CCR-18.title: Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA)
CCR-18.one_screen: CVA is the adjustment to the fair value of a derivative portfolio reflecting the counterparty’s credit risk. It is effectively the market value of expected loss from counterparty default, similar to “credit spread” on the portfolio. Banks include CVA in pricing and may hold hedges for it.

sources.label: Federal Reserve et al., “Interagency Guidance” (definition of CVA).
BCBS “CVA framework” (Basel III adjustments).

CCR-19.title: Debit Valuation Adjustment (DVA) and Funding Costs
CCR-19.one_screen: DVA is the opposite of CVA: it is the value adjustment reflecting the bank’s own credit risk on its liabilities. In practice, DVA means the bank would mark a gain if its own credit spread widens (bad for stakeholders but accounting shows a profit). DVA is controversial because it ties reported earnings to the bank’s health.

sources.label: Accounting Standards (IFRS 13/ASC 820) for CVA/DVA definitions.
FVA/MVA discussions (e.g. Risk.net tutorials).

CCR-20.title: FVA, MVA, KVA and the XVA Family
CCR-20.one_screen: Beyond CVA and DVA, a suite of valuation adjustments (XVAs) addresses other costs. The key ones are: Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA), Margin Valuation Adjustment (MVA), and Capital Valuation Adjustment (KVA). FVA is the cost of funding collateral flows. MVA is specifically the cost of funding initial margin. KVA is a charge reflecting the cost of holding regulatory capital. These are mainly used in internal pricing rather than capital rules.

sources.label: Emanuel Derman, et al., “Beyond the Black Box: XVAs in Practice” (journal articles).
Risk.net XVA Primer.

CCR-21.title: CVA Capital Charge
CCR-21.one_screen: Capital rules specify methodologies for CVA capital. Basel 3.1 (Basel IV) replaced the Advanced CVA approach with two standardized approaches: a “standardized approach for CVA” (SA-CVA) using risk weights on counterparty exposures and CDS spreads, and a “basic approach” (BA-CVA) using broad factors. Under SA-CVA, a bank computes a regulatory CVA VaR or formula-based capital based on net exposures, counterparty risk weights, and allows limited hedge recognition. The details are complex and specified in regulatory texts. In all approaches, recognized CVA hedges (single-name CDS or index) can reduce capital, up to 50% by Basel rules.

sources.label: Basel Committee, “CVA risk framework” (Mar 2023).
UK PRA PS17/23 (Basel 3.1 CVA rules).
EU Commission CRR3 text (2023).

CCR-22.title: Settlement vs Pre-Settlement Risk
CCR-22.one_screen: Pre-settlement risk is the counterparty credit risk during the life of a trade (as described above). Settlement risk (often called Herstatt risk in FX) is the risk that one party pays while the other does not at settlement time, usually due to timing differences. For instance, in an FX trade across time zones, a bank may deliver EUR but not yet receive USD if the counterparty fails.

sources.label: Dirk Bullmann, “FX settlement risk: to PvP or not to PvP” (CLS, 2023).
FX Global Code (2017) on PvP recommendations.

CCR-23.title: Basel Framework (Global Standard)
CCR-23.one_screen: The Basel Committee’s published standards (Basel III, Basel 3.1, etc.) are the definitive source for CCR methodologies and capital. Key texts include BCBS 279 (SA-CCR standard) and the Basel III Revised Framework for market risk/CVA. These set the universal baseline for capital and definitions in all jurisdictions.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, “The standardised approach for measuring CCR exposures” (Mar 2014).
BCBS “Credit Valuation Adjustment” final framework (2023).

CCR-24.title: UK/EU Implementation
CCR-24.one_screen: The UK and EU have adopted Basel CCR and CVA rules through their capital regulations. The EU’s CRR3 (part of Basel 3.1 package) was agreed in late 2023 and takes effect Jan 1, 2025. It includes SA-CCR for calculating exposures and the new standardized CVA capital approach. The UK’s PRA released draft standards (PS17/23) on CCR/CVA, finalizing them for implementation by July 2025.

sources.label: UK PRA Policy Statement PS17/23 (Apr 2024).
EU CRR3 Regulation (EU 2023/xxx) and EBA guidelines. (See press releases).

CCR-25.title: India’s CCR Regulation
CCR-25.one_screen: The RBI currently uses Basel III’s CCR guidance but has not fully adopted SA-CCR yet. In India, the Basel III Capital Regulations (Master Circular) still prescribe the Current Exposure Method (CEM) with updated add-on factors. In August 2025 RBI invited comments on revisions to CEM add-ons in its Basel III circular. It has indicated a phased move towards SA-CCR after FY26–27 (2026–27), subject to market readiness (industry sources).

sources.label: RBI Master Circular on Basel III Capital (2025) (CCR guidelines, CEM usage).
IL IndiaLaw LLP / Mondaq (Aug 2025) (on RBI’s CCR draft and move towards Basel alignment).
CCIL website (IRS clearing) (India’s CCP).

CCR-26.title: US CCR Regulation
CCR-26.one_screen: The US banking regulators have implemented SA-CCR for U.S. banks. A final rule (Nov 2019) required bank holding companies and large banks to use SA-CCR for derivatives exposures (effective April 2020, with mandatory compliance by Jan 2022). This rule also updated hedging recognition and collateral treatment. For CVA, the U.S. agencies in late 2022 released proposals to revise the CVA capital charge in line with Basel, but no final rule is in force yet.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, OCC, FDIC press release (Nov 2019) (SA-CCR final rule).
U.S. Federal Register (proposed CCR/CVA rule) (2022).

CR-01.title: Obligor, borrower and counterparty
CR-01.one_screen: Credit risk attaches to a person that owes performance, not to a customer label. **Obligor** identifies the legal or natural person responsible for the credit obligation; **borrower** and **counterparty** describe roles that may coincide with the obligor but need not.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BCBS d595, *Principles for the Management of Credit Risk*, 30 April 2025
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, CRE50, *Counterparty credit risk definitions and terminology*

CR-02.title: Product, facility and account
CR-02.one_screen: A product is a reusable lending design, a facility is a specific contractual grant of credit, and an account is an operational record used to book and service activity. Credit risk measures become ambiguous unless they declare which level they attach to.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BCBS d595, *Principles for the Management of Credit Risk*, 30 April 2025
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, CRE36, *IRB approach: minimum requirements to use IRB approach*

CR-03.title: Exposure and aggregation levels
CR-03.one_screen: Exposure is the amount or value subject to credit loss for a stated purpose; it is not automatically today’s drawn balance. The same relationship can produce different valid exposure numbers at account, facility, obligor, connected-group and portfolio levels.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025*, 28 November 2025.
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, CRE32, *IRB approach: risk components*
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, CRE36, *IRB approach: minimum requirements to use IRB approach*

CR-04.title: Connected counterparties and economic groups
CR-04.one_screen: Legal separation does not guarantee independent credit risk. Connected-counterparty analysis aggregates persons when control or economic interdependence creates a common failure channel, so one concentrated risk cannot be disguised as several names.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, LEX10, *Definitions and application*
Prudential Regulation Authority, SS3/25, *Identification of groups of connected clients*, 17 July 2025
Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, 12 CFR Part 32, *Lending Limits*.

CR-05.title: Underwriting and the credit decision
CR-05.one_screen: Underwriting converts information about the obligor, facility and environment into a governed decision to approve, decline or reshape credit. The decision starts with a sustainable **primary source of repayment**; collateral and guarantees can reduce loss if repayment fails, but they do not repair weak repayment capacity.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BCBS d595, *Principles for the Management of Credit Risk*, 30 April 2025
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework, BCP40, *The Core Principles and assessment criteria*
European Banking Authority, EBA/GL/2020/06, *Guidelines on loan origination and monitoring*, 29 May 2020.

CR-06.title: Collateral, security and guarantees
CR-06.one_screen: Collateral, security interests and guarantees are credit-risk mitigants only to the extent that the bank can legally rely on them and realise value when needed. Their underwriting job is to provide a credible **secondary way out**; their later LGD role is separate and depends on realised recovery cash flows.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, BCBS d595, *Principles for the Management of Credit Risk*, 30 April 2025

CR-07.title: Default: defining the event
CR-07.one_screen: Default is a governed credit state, not a synonym for arrears, loss, bankruptcy or write-off. Every PD, default rate, cure rate and LGD inherits the unit and events used in the default definition, so the event must be fixed before the metric.

CR-08.title: Arrears, days past due and delinquency states
CR-08.one_screen: Arrears measure unpaid contractual amounts; days past due measure how long payment has remained unpaid; delinquency buckets convert that clock into operational states. These are payment facts, not loss estimates or the complete definition of default.

CR-09.title: Unlikeliness to pay
CR-09.one_screen: Unlikeliness to pay identifies default from the substance of credit deterioration before a delinquency clock necessarily reaches its backstop. It asks whether full payment remains likely without extraordinary recovery action; it is governed judgement, not a discretionary weakness label.

CR-11.title: Restructuring, forbearance and distressed concessions
CR-11.one_screen: Restructuring changes contractual terms; forbearance is a concession associated with the debtor’s financial difficulty. A modification can preserve value, but cannot erase the deterioration that made the original terms unsustainable.

CR-12.title: Cure, probation and re-default
CR-12.one_screen: Cure is the governed transition from default back to non-default after the default conditions have ceased and renewed performance is credible. Re-default is a later return to default; a temporary payment or zero-DPD snapshot is not enough to prove a durable cure.

CR-13.title: Write-off, recovery and economic loss
CR-13.one_screen: Write-off changes the carrying amount or prudential treatment of an exposure; recovery records value collected after credit failure; economic loss measures what was ultimately lost after recoveries, costs and timing. None of these events should erase the default lifecycle that produced them.

CR-14.title: Probability of default
CR-14.one_screen: Probability of default is the probability that a defined obligor, facility or pool enters a defined default state over a specified future horizon, conditional on information available at an observation date. A number labelled “PD” is incomplete until its **unit, event, horizon and conditioning information** are known.

CR-15.title: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle PD
CR-15.one_screen: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle describe how strongly a rating or PD responds to current versus cyclical conditions. They are conditioning philosophies on a spectrum, not synonyms for short-horizon and long-horizon probability.

CR-16.title: Loss given default and recovery rate
CR-16.one_screen: Loss given default is loss severity **conditional on default**. Collateral and guarantees influence LGD only through legally available, economically realised recovery value; an appraisal at origination is therefore an input to recovery expectations, not the LGD itself.

CR-17.title: Exposure at default and credit conversion factors
CR-17.one_screen: Exposure at default estimates or prescribes how much is exposed when default occurs, not how much is drawn today. Credit conversion factors translate undrawn or contingent amounts into exposure, making pre-default utilisation behaviour part of credit risk.

CR-18.title: Expected loss: PD × LGD × EAD
CR-18.one_screen: `EL = PD × LGD × EAD` is a compact one-period loss decomposition only when the three inputs describe compatible default events, horizons, populations and economic conditions. The arithmetic is trivial; parameter alignment is the real mechanism.

CR-19.title: Retail versus wholesale credit modelling
CR-19.one_screen: Retail credit is usually managed through large pools of comparatively homogeneous exposures, making repeated statistical patterns powerful evidence. Wholesale credit is usually more obligor-centred because exposures are larger, populations are smaller and borrower-specific financial, structural and legal information matters more.

CR-20.title: Application, behavioural and bureau credit data
CR-20.one_screen: Application models use information available at or before origination; behavioural models use information generated after the relationship exists; bureau or credit-information data add externally reported indebtedness and repayment history. Their common discipline is **time**: only information genuinely available at the decision or observation date may enter the prediction.

CR-21.title: Rating grades, master scales and migration
CR-21.one_screen: A rating grade is a discrete class of borrower credit quality; a master scale defines the ordered meaning of all grades; migration records movement through that scale over time. A grade is not meaningful because it is called “4” or “BBB-like”—its meaning comes from assignment criteria, ordering, default boundary and calibrated risk.

CR-22.title: Vintage analysis and roll rates
CR-22.one_screen: Vintage analysis follows exposures originated at similar times as they season; roll-rate analysis follows movement between delinquency or credit states. Both restore the time dimension that a portfolio snapshot destroys.

sources.label: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, *Estimation Methodologies for Losses, Revenues, and Expenses*, August 2013

CR-23.title: Concentration and diversification
CR-23.one_screen: Concentration risk arises when too much exposure depends on the same name, connected group, sector, geography, collateral type or underlying economic driver. Diversification comes from genuinely different sources of loss, not from the number of rows, facilities or legal entities in a dataset.

CR-24.title: Correlation and systematic credit risk
CR-24.one_screen: Credit correlation means default and loss outcomes are not independent because common economic forces move many borrowers together. Idiosyncratic risk can be diversified across sufficiently independent exposures; systematic risk cannot be removed by adding more borrowers exposed to the same underlying conditions.

CR-25.title: Unexpected loss and capital
CR-25.one_screen: Expected loss is the average credit cost under a defined measurement; unexpected loss is adverse variation around that average. Capital protects solvency against sufficiently severe outcomes above ordinary expected-loss capacity, so portfolio dispersion and dependence matter even when exposure-level EL is unchanged.

CR-26.title: The credit-loss architecture
CR-26.one_screen: Credit risk is one continuous system: identify the person and exposure, decide whether repayment is sustainable, recognise default consistently, measure probability, severity and exposure, then aggregate common loss drivers into portfolio tail risk. The architecture fails when adjacent layers are collapsed—for example, collateral into repayment capacity, DPD into default, score into PD, or expected loss into capital.

DAT-01.title: Risk Data as a Discipline
DAT-01.one_screen: In the 2007–2009 financial crisis, banks could not aggregate their risk exposures quickly or accurately. This failure impaired timely decision-making, prompting regulators to formalize risk data management as a discipline (e.g. Basel BCBS 239) to ensure banks maintain accurate, timely, end-to-end risk data aggregation and reporting.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting*, Jan 2013.
Basel Committee press release, *Progress report on BCBS 239 implementation* (28 Nov 2023).

DAT-02.title: Risk Data Aggregation vs Risk Reporting
DAT-02.one_screen: Risk data aggregation is the internal process of collecting and consolidating all relevant risk data across the bank. Risk reporting is the output of that process, conveying the aggregated data in reports. BCBS 239 treats them as separate obligations: the former ensures data is accurate and complete; the latter ensures reports are clear and delivered on time.

sources.label: FluxForce, *BCBS 239: What It Requires* (2026).

DAT-03.title: BCBS 239 Principles Overview
DAT-03.one_screen: BCBS 239 comprises 14 principles organized in four groups: (I) Governance & Infrastructure (board accountability, data architecture), (II) Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (accuracy, completeness, timeliness, adaptability), (III) Risk Reporting Practices (comprehensiveness, clarity, frequency, distribution), and (IV) Supervisory Review (how regulators assess banks). Together they form a principles-based framework requiring banks to implement robust data policies and systems.

sources.label: Basel Committee, *Principles for effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting*, Jan 2013.
FluxForce, *BCBS 239: Requirements, Scope & Compliance* (2026).
Basel Committee press release (28 Nov 2023).

DAT-04.title: Risk Data Aggregation Capabilities (Accuracy, Completeness, Timeliness, Adaptability)
DAT-04.one_screen: BCBS 239 mandates that a bank’s risk data aggregation be **accurate, complete, timely, and adaptable**. In practice, this means automated data pipelines, extensive reconciliations, and flexible reporting capabilities. Banks must reconcile risk data with accounting records, cover ~95% of exposures across all entities, refresh data fast (daily or intraday for critical metrics), and be able to run ad-hoc reports on demand.

DAT-05.title: Risk Reporting Practices
DAT-05.one_screen: BCBS 239 requires risk reports to be **accurate, comprehensive, clear, frequent, and properly distributed**. Reports must be tailored to their audience (e.g. board vs risk manager) and sufficiently granular. This ensures stakeholders get the right information at the right time.

sources.label: FluxForce, *BCBS 239 Principles* (2026).

DAT-06.title: Supervisory Review and Compliance Record
DAT-06.one_screen: The final BCBS 239 principles cover supervisory review (Principles 12–14) and require banks to act on regulators’ findings. By 2023, global reports show banks remain at “different stages” of compliance and need significant work to meet the standard.

sources.label: Basel Committee press release (28 Nov 2023).
FluxForce, *BCBS 239 Compliance* (2026).

DAT-07.title: Golden Source of Data
DAT-07.one_screen: A golden source is the single authoritative source of truth for a given data element across the organization. It contains the most accurate and up-to-date version of that data, and all systems reference this “one source” to avoid discrepancies.

sources.label: Raw Knowledge blog, *Golden Source of Data* (2022).
Basel Committee BCBS 239, Principle 2 (data architecture).

DAT-08.title: Critical Data Elements (CDEs)
DAT-08.one_screen: Critical Data Elements (CDEs) are the data points an organization deems essential to its core operations, decision-making, and compliance. In banking, CDEs include fields like customer ID, credit exposure amounts, collateral valuations, etc. They require special governance attention since errors in CDEs can have significant impact.

sources.label: Alation blog, *Critical Data Elements Explained* (Feb 2025).

DAT-09.title: Data Lineage (Business vs Technical)
DAT-09.one_screen: Data lineage tracks the journey of data from its origin to its final use. *Business lineage* is a high-level, user-friendly map of what data comes from where for reporting purposes; *technical lineage* is the detailed breakdown of data flows through systems and code. Both are essential for understanding and troubleshooting data issues.

sources.label: Secoda blog, *Business vs Technical Data Lineage* (Dec 2024).

DAT-10.title: Metadata and Business Glossary
DAT-10.one_screen: Metadata is “data about data” – information that defines and describes data elements. A business glossary is a centralized catalog of business terms and their definitions. Together, they ensure everyone has a common understanding of data definitions.

sources.label: RBI Committee Report on Data Standardization, *Executive Summary* (2018).

DAT-11.title: Data Dictionary and Data Model
DAT-11.one_screen: A data dictionary is a detailed catalog of all fields (data elements), describing each one’s attributes (name, type, description, format, valid values, etc.). A data model (conceptual or logical) is a diagram showing entities and relationships between them. Together they help design systems and prevent misinterpretation.

sources.label: RudderStack blog, *What is a Data Dictionary?* (Jan 2025).

DAT-12.title: Reference Data vs Master Data
DAT-12.one_screen: Master data consists of core business entities (e.g. customers, accounts, products) that are critical to operations, while reference data consists of standardized code sets or classifications (e.g. country codes, currency codes, security identifiers). Master data changes as business grows; reference data is relatively stable and often global (ISO codes, etc.).

sources.label: Dataversity, *Master Data vs Reference Data* (Apr 2024).

DAT-13.title: Data Quality Dimensions
DAT-13.one_screen: Data quality is multi-dimensional. Key dimensions include **accuracy** (data correctly reflects reality), **completeness** (no missing values), **consistency** (data aligns across sources), **timeliness** (data is up-to-date and available when needed), **validity** (data follows defined formats and rules), and **uniqueness** (no duplicates).

sources.label: Raw Knowledge blog, *Golden Source of Data* (2022).

DAT-14.title: Data Quality Rules, Thresholds, and Exception Management
DAT-14.one_screen: Data quality rules are specific checks or constraints (e.g. “loan amount ≥ 0”, “interest date must not precede loan date”). Thresholds set acceptable levels for quality metrics (e.g. “95% of records must be complete”). When data fails a rule or threshold, it is flagged as an exception to be investigated and resolved.

sources.label: Generic best practice (no specific cite).

DAT-15.title: Reconciliation (Front-to-Back and Risk-to-Finance)
DAT-15.one_screen: Reconciliation is the process of comparing data between systems to detect and resolve differences. *Front-to-back* reconciliation ensures that transactions recorded in front-office systems (trading, loans booking) match entries in the back-office accounting system. *Risk-to-finance* reconciliation ensures that risk metrics (e.g. aggregated exposures) reconcile to financial accounts (e.g. total assets or regulatory capital). Both are critical controls for data integrity.

sources.label: Industry practice (Capgemini blog) (conceptual).
Regulatory expectation (implied by BCBS 239 emphasis on accuracy/integrity).

DAT-16.title: Data Ownership vs Stewardship
DAT-16.one_screen: **Data owners** are senior business managers who are accountable for data assets; **data stewards** are specialists who manage data quality day-to-day. The owner defines data policies and sets quality standards, while the steward implements these standards and handles operational issues.

sources.label: RBI Committee Report on Data Governance (2018).

DAT-17.title: Data Governance Models
DAT-17.one_screen: Data governance models define how oversight is structured. Common models are *centralized* (a single data governance committee sets policies for all) and *federated* (each business unit has its own governance under corporate guidelines). RBI notes typical models based on process, subject area, or geography, but emphasizes business-function-based ownership.

sources.label: RBI Committee Report on Data Governance (2018).

DAT-18.title: Issue Management and Remediation
DAT-18.one_screen: Data issues must be formally managed: identified, tracked, and remediated through a controlled process. This typically involves logging issues in an issue-tracking system, prioritizing by severity, performing root-cause analysis, and implementing fixes under governance oversight.

sources.label: Industry practice (implied by regulatory expectations).

DAT-19.title: Regulatory Returns and Production Cycle
DAT-19.one_screen: A *regulatory return* is a standardized report or form that banks must submit to supervisors (e.g. capital, liquidity, or risk data). The production cycle involves: extracting data from source systems, transforming and mapping it to the return’s schema, aggregating as needed, validating the report against business rules, then submitting and attesting.

sources.label: Regnology, *India Element-Based Reporting (EBR) explained*. (Context on RBI’s focus.)
Standard industry practice.

DAT-20.title: Attestation, Restatements, and Reporting Change Programs
DAT-20.one_screen: **Attestation and sign-off:** Senior management (often the board, CEO or Chief Risk Officer) must formally attest that each regulatory report is accurate and complete. This is both a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and an internal control. **Restatements:** If a material error is discovered after submission, the bank must correct (“restatement”) the return. Restatements can impact capital calculations or regulatory standings, so timely correction and explanation are critical. **Reporting change programs:** When regulations change or new reports are added, a change program is launched. This involves requirement analysis, mapping updates, system development, testing, and parallel runs.

sources.label: Common regulatory practice (e.g. RBI circulars).

DAT-21.title: Delivery Layer: Requirements, Mapping, and Testing
DAT-21.one_screen: The delivery layer in a data program consists of business requirements, mapping specifications, and testing. A Business Requirements Document (BRD) defines *what* reports/data are needed (with business context). A Data Mapping Specification details *how* each target field is derived from source fields with transformation logic. Testing involves pre-defined result sets and user acceptance testing (UAT) to validate that the implemented mappings produce the expected outputs.

sources.label: Standard project practice (no specific citation).

DAT-22.one_screen: Regulatory reporting frameworks differ by jurisdiction. BCBS 239 itself is a global set of principles with **no direct legal force**. In practice:

FND-01.title: Bank as a Balance Sheet
FND-01.one_screen: A bank is a balance sheet before it is a building, app, or lender. It owns assets, owes liabilities, and has equity equal to the residual difference: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting*, Chapters 4–5

FND-02.title: Deposits and Loans: Opposite Sides of the Bank
FND-02.one_screen: **Deposits fund the bank and are liabilities; loans use the bank's balance sheet and are assets.** The words are usually spoken from the customer's perspective, which is why beginners instinctively put them on the wrong sides.

sources.label: Bank of England, *How is money created?*, Explainer

FND-03.title: Loan Creation, Deposits and Funding
FND-03.one_screen: When a bank grants a loan and credits the borrower's account, it can create a **loan asset and a deposit liability simultaneously**. That does not make funding irrelevant: payments out of the bank create settlement outflows, while liquidity, capital, risk and profitability constrain sustainable lending.

FND-04.title: Net Interest Income and Bank Earnings
FND-04.one_screen: A traditional bank earns a spread by receiving interest on interest-earning assets and paying interest on funding. **Net interest income = interest income − interest expense**, but final profit also reflects fees, market-related income, operating expenses, credit losses and taxes.

sources.label: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, *Banking System Conditions*, Supervision and Regulation Report, November 2023

FND-05.title: Capital Versus Liquidity
FND-05.one_screen: **Capital absorbs losses; liquidity meets payments when due.** A bank can have positive capital yet fail through a cash shortage, or hold abundant cash yet be economically insolvent because its assets are worth less than its obligations.

FND-06.title: The Financial Statements and How They Link
FND-06.one_screen: The three-statement shorthand is **balance sheet, profit and loss statement, and cash-flow statement**. Profit changes equity, cash flows explain movements in cash, and every recognised closing balance must end up on the closing balance sheet.

FND-07.title: Reading a Bank Balance Sheet
FND-07.one_screen: Read a bank balance sheet by asking three questions in order: **what assets generate or preserve value, how those assets are funded, and how much residual loss absorption sits beneath the liabilities**. A bank's debtors are often its customers, while its customers' deposits are its funding.

FND-08.title: Accrual Versus Cash
FND-08.one_screen: **Accrual accounting recognises economic effects when the recognition criteria are met, not simply when cash moves.** Cash accounting asks when money moved; accrual accounting asks what asset, liability, income or expense exists because of what happened.

FND-09.title: Provisions and Credit-Loss Allowances
FND-09.one_screen: A credit-loss allowance recognises that the amount expected to be collected from credit exposures may be less than their contractual amount. **The economic idea is shared; the recognition and measurement rule is jurisdiction- and reporting-framework-specific.**

FND-10.title: Other Comprehensive Income
FND-10.one_screen: **Other comprehensive income (OCI) is a reporting route for specified recognised income and expense that the applicable accounting standard does not put in current profit or loss.** It is not "less real" income, and it is not a discretionary parking place for inconvenient volatility.

FND-11.title: Present Value and Discount Factors
FND-11.one_screen: **Present value converts money at different dates into values at one common date.** A discount factor is the multiplier that performs that conversion: for one annual rate \(r\), the time-\(t\) factor is \(1/(1+r)^t\).

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix B, including B5.5.44 on discounting expected credit losses

FND-12.title: Compounding and Discounting Conventions
FND-12.one_screen: **Compounding moves value forward through time; discounting moves it backward.** The mathematics only works when the rate, compounding frequency, day-count or period convention, and cash-flow dates are internally consistent.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A and application guidance on effective interest calculations

FND-13.title: Effective Interest Rate
FND-13.one_screen: The **effective interest rate (EIR)** is the single periodic rate that makes the present value of the relevant contractual cash-flow stream equal to the instrument's initial carrying amount under the stated methodology. It converts price, interest, fees and timing into one internally consistent yield.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A, effective interest method and effective interest rate definitions

FND-14.title: NPV and Discounting Expected Loss
FND-14.one_screen: **Net present value (NPV) adds cash flows after converting them to one valuation date.** Expected loss is time-sensitive when the applicable methodology discounts shortfalls: the same nominal shortfall occurring later has a different present value.

FND-15.title: Exposure: What Is Actually at Risk
FND-15.one_screen: **Exposure is the amount or position whose value can be affected by a risk event; it is not the loss itself.** The relevant exposure may include more than today's booked principal because commitments, accrued amounts, derivatives or future drawings can also be at risk.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Basel Framework — Credit Risk*, consolidated framework

FND-16.title: Probability and Expected Value
FND-16.one_screen: **Probability says how likely an outcome is; expected value combines each possible outcome with its probability.** A 1% probability of losing 100 is not a loss of 1%, but in a two-outcome example it contributes an expected loss of 1.

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods*

FND-17.title: Variance and Volatility
FND-17.one_screen: **Variance measures average squared dispersion around a mean; standard deviation is its square root.** In finance, volatility usually refers to a standard-deviation measure over a stated horizon, so volatility is meaningless without the variable, data frequency and time horizon.

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Measures of Scale*, Section 1.3.5.6
