FND-18.title: Quantiles and Tail Risk
FND-18.one_screen: A **quantile** is a threshold in a distribution: an \(\alpha\)-quantile has approximately \(\alpha\) of probability at or below it under the stated convention. **Tail risk is what happens in the extreme region beyond such thresholds; a quantile is not a maximum possible loss.**

sources.label: National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Percentiles and Critical Values*
National Institute of Standards and Technology, *NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — Distributional Shape and Tails*

FND-19.title: Expected Loss Versus Unexpected Loss
FND-19.one_screen: **Expected loss is the probability-weighted average loss built into the centre of the loss distribution; unexpected loss is adverse variation around and beyond that expectation.** Provisioning and pricing address expected loss in different ways, while prudential capital is fundamentally concerned with resilience to losses beyond the expected level.

FND-20.title: Risk Appetite
FND-20.one_screen: **Risk appetite is the aggregate level and types of risk an institution is willing to assume within its risk capacity while pursuing its objectives.** Appetite becomes operational only when translated into limits, monitored against the actual risk profile, and linked to escalation and decisions.

sources.label: Financial Stability Board, *Principles for an Effective Risk Appetite Framework*, November 18, 2013

FND-21.title: The Three Lines Model
FND-21.one_screen: The Three Lines Model separates **management's ownership and management of risk**, specialist support and challenge, and **independent internal-audit assurance**. The lines are roles in governance, not walls that permit one function to outsource responsibility to another.

FND-22.title: Policy, Standard and Procedure
FND-22.one_screen: A useful control hierarchy is **policy = required intent and principles; standard = mandatory control or design criteria; procedure = steps for execution**. The terminology is not legally universal, so authority and content matter more than the document label.

FND-23.title: What a Regulator Actually Does
FND-23.one_screen: A banking regulator turns law and statutory objectives into enforceable boundaries, while **supervision** tests how institutions actually operate inside those boundaries. Depending on the mandate, the toolkit can include authorisation, rules, reporting, examinations, remediation and enforcement.

FND-24.title: Prudential Regulation, Conduct Regulation and Accounting Standards
FND-24.one_screen: **Prudential regulation asks whether a financial institution is safe and resilient; conduct regulation asks whether it behaves properly toward customers and markets; accounting standards determine how financial position and performance are recognised, measured and reported.** The three systems interact, but none is a substitute for another.

IMP-01.title: Impairment and Expected Credit Loss
IMP-01.one_screen: Impairment is the accounting recognition that contractual credit cash flows will not all be collected. Expected-credit-loss accounting brings that recognition forward: the allowance reflects losses expected from credit risk before a loss event has necessarily occurred.

IMP-02.title: Credit Loss Is a Discounted Cash Shortfall
IMP-02.one_screen: Under IFRS 9, credit loss is fundamentally the present value of the difference between contractual cash flows due and cash flows expected to be received. PD, LGD and EAD are modelling components; the accounting target is the cash shortfall.

IMP-03.title: Probability-Weighted Outcomes
IMP-03.one_screen: ECL is an expectation across possible credit outcomes, not the loss under the single scenario management considers most likely. Non-linearity matters: weighting scenario-specific losses can differ materially from calculating loss once at probability-weighted average macroeconomic inputs.

IMP-04.title: Effective Interest Rate Discounting
IMP-04.one_screen: IFRS 9 discounts expected cash shortfalls using the effective interest rate established from the instrument’s own economics, not a current market yield selected at the reporting date. The rule prevents changes in market discount rates from being mistaken for changes in credit loss.

IMP-05.title: Forward-Looking Information and Macroeconomic Scenarios
IMP-05.one_screen: ECL must respond to information about the future when that information is relevant, reasonable and supportable. Macroeconomic forecasts are inputs to credit-risk expectations, not independent reserves added on top of modelled loss.

IMP-06.title: The IFRS 9 Three-Stage Architecture
IMP-06.one_screen: IFRS 9 staging changes the horizon of loss recognition as credit risk changes: Stage 1 carries 12-month ECL, Stage 2 lifetime ECL after significant deterioration, and Stage 3 lifetime ECL once the asset is credit-impaired. Stage is a credit-risk state, not simply an arrears bucket.

IMP-07.title: Twelve-Month ECL
IMP-07.one_screen: Twelve-month ECL is not the cash loss expected during the next twelve months. It is the lifetime credit loss arising from default events that are possible within the next twelve months, weighted by the probability of those defaults.

IMP-08.title: Significant Increase in Credit Risk
IMP-08.one_screen: SICR is principally a relative test: compare the risk of default over the remaining life at the reporting date with that risk at initial recognition. Absolute thresholds can operationalise or conservatively supplement the test, but they must not erase the origination benchmark.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, paragraphs 5.5.9–5.5.11 and B5.5.5–B5.5.23

IMP-09.title: The Thirty-Day Past-Due Backstop
IMP-09.one_screen: More than 30 days past due creates a rebuttable IFRS 9 presumption that SICR has occurred. It is a backstop, not the normal definition of Stage 2, and rebuttal requires reasonable and supportable evidence rather than routine policy.

IMP-10.title: Stage Three and Credit-Impaired Assets
IMP-10.one_screen: Stage 3 means the financial asset is credit-impaired at the reporting date, not merely that its risk has increased. Lifetime ECL remains the allowance basis, while IFRS 9 changes interest recognition for assets that became credit-impaired after origination.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A, paragraph 5.4.1 and B5.5.37

IMP-11.title: Purchased or Originated Credit-Impaired Assets
IMP-11.one_screen: A POCI asset is already credit-impaired when first recognised, so ordinary Stage 1-to-Stage 3 logic does not describe its economics. IFRS 9 embeds initial expected credit losses in a credit-adjusted EIR and subsequently recognises only changes in lifetime ECL.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, Appendix A, paragraphs 5.4.1 and 5.5.13–5.5.14

IMP-12.title: Transfers Back and Cure Asymmetry
IMP-12.one_screen: IFRS 9 allows transfer back from lifetime to 12-month ECL when the SICR criterion is no longer met, but reversal is not simply the mirror image of deterioration. The question is whether current lifetime default risk is no longer significantly above the origination benchmark—not whether the latest adverse symptom has merely disappeared.

IMP-13.title: Lifetime PD Term Structures
IMP-13.one_screen: Lifetime ECL needs the timing of default risk, not merely one lifetime default percentage. Marginal PD measures default probability in a particular future interval conditional on survival to that interval; cumulative PD measures the probability of having defaulted by a stated horizon.

sources.label: IFRS Foundation, *IFRS 9 Financial Instruments*, paragraphs B5.5.10–B5.5.13

IMP-14.title: Lifetime EAD and Revolving Behavioural Life
IMP-14.one_screen: Lifetime EAD is a path through time, not today’s balance copied into every future period. Revolving facilities are special because future drawdowns and the period of credit exposure can depend on borrower behaviour and the lender’s practical risk-management actions, sometimes extending beyond a nominal cancellation notice period.

IMP-15.title: Accounting LGD Versus Regulatory LGD
IMP-15.one_screen: Accounting LGD estimates the loss severity needed to satisfy an accounting ECL measurement objective; regulatory LGD is calibrated for prudential capital objectives. Regulatory parameters can be useful starting points, but they are not interchangeable because horizon, cyclicality, conservatism and prescribed floors can differ.

IMP-16.title: Overlays and Post-Model Adjustments
IMP-16.one_screen: An overlay or post-model adjustment changes model output when relevant credit risk is not adequately captured by the model. It is necessary when models have known blind spots, but dangerous when it becomes an undocumented plug, double-counts modelled risk or persists after the underlying deficiency should have been repaired.

IMP-17.title: ECL Model Validation and Backtesting
IMP-17.one_screen: Validation asks whether an ECL model is conceptually sound, implemented correctly and performing acceptably for its intended accounting use. Backtesting is one part of validation: compare predictions with realised outcomes, diagnose differences, and determine whether recalibration, redevelopment or a controlled adjustment is needed.

IMP-18.title: Staging Validation and ECL Disclosures
IMP-18.one_screen: Staging needs its own validation because a well-calibrated PD model can still produce wrong allowances if SICR thresholds move exposures too early or too late. Disclosures then make the framework observable by explaining staging policies, assumptions, forward-looking information, allowance movements and credit-risk concentrations.

IMP-19.title: US CECL Under ASC 326
IMP-19.one_screen: CECL and IFRS 9 are both forward-looking expected-loss frameworks, but CECL is not “IFRS 9 without stage labels”. For amortised-cost assets, CECL recognises lifetime expected credit losses from initial recognition, eliminating the IFRS 9 SICR gateway between 12-month and lifetime ECL.

IMP-20.title: India: IRACP, Ind AS and the Bank ECL Transition
IMP-20.one_screen: India must be read as three distinct tracks: scheduled commercial banks are not on Ind AS and remain under RBI IRACP through March 31, 2027; relevant NBFCs already apply Ind AS, including Ind AS 109 ECL; and RBI has issued a separate final three-stage ECL framework for commercial banks that becomes effective April 1, 2027. The January 2023 ECL discussion paper was a proposal; the April 2026 Directions are final future rules, not current rules as of August 28, 2026.

IND-01.title: RBI’s Mandate and Dual Role
IND-01.one_screen: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India’s central bank with a broad mandate that goes beyond prudential supervision. In addition to setting monetary policy and ensuring banking stability, RBI has a statutory “developmental role” – promoting national objectives like financial inclusion and credit to agriculture and MSMEs.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India – “Organisation and Functions” (official).
RBI Financial Inclusion & Development Overview (section on PSL).

IND-02.title: Bank Categories in India (SCB, SFB, Payments, RRB, Coop)
IND-02.one_screen: India’s banking system has multiple specialized categories.  *Scheduled Commercial Banks* (SCBs) – including public, private, foreign, regional rural, scheduled payments banks, small finance banks, and co-operative banks – have broad banking powers. Small Finance Banks focus on underserved segments; Payments Banks can take small deposits but cannot lend.  Co-operative banks and RRBs serve member or rural communities with limited geographic scope.

sources.label: Ministry of Finance FAQs on banks.
RBI Master Directions (payments banks) (deposit limit for PB).

IND-03.title: NBFC Scale-Based Regulation (SBR)
IND-03.one_screen: In 2022–2023, RBI moved to a four-tier, size-and-risk-based regulatory framework for NBFCs. The framework classifies NBFCs into Base, Middle, Upper and Top layers. Base-layer NBFCs are the smallest/non-deposit ones (assets < ₹1,000 crore) and fintech entities; middle-layer NBFCs include deposit-taking companies and larger NBFCs (assets ≥ ₹1,000 cr) and critical segments like HFCs, CICs, etc.; Upper and Top layers (ideally empty) are for systemically important NBFCs subject to enhanced scrutiny.

sources.label: RBI (2022) – Master Directions on NBFC – SBR framework.

IND-04.title: Housing Finance Companies under RBI
IND-04.one_screen: As of August 2019, Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) were brought under RBI’s regulation. The Central Bank is now the regulator of HFCs (lenders specializing in home loans), integrating them into the NBFC framework.  During the transition, HFCs were allowed to follow existing NHB guidelines until RBI issues new rules.

sources.label: RBI Press Release (Aug 13, 2019) on transfer of HFC regulation.

IND-05.title: Banks vs. NBFCs: Key Distinctions
IND-05.one_screen: Commercial banks and NBFCs in India differ in core functions and regulation.  Banks can accept demand deposits, offer cheque facilities, and participate in the payment system – NBFCs cannot.  NBFCs rely mostly on wholesale/market funding or term deposits (for deposit-taking NBFCs).  Banks have RBI-backed deposit insurance (DICGC cover), maintain CRR/SLR, and access RBI liquidity; NBFCs do not (except selective refinance schemes).  Banks require higher entry capital and stricter licensing; NBFCs have a lower ₹2 crore equity norm but face similar prudential norms scaled to their assets.  Because NBFCs cannot create money via demand deposits, their funding costs and leverage limits differ fundamentally from banks.

sources.label: RBI Act definitions and NBFC Directions (general principle).
RBI FAQs and master directions (see [25], [51]).

IND-06.title: Asset Classification and NPA Norms (IRACP)
IND-06.one_screen: Banks must classify each loan into Standard, Sub-standard, Doubtful or Loss assets based on repayment delays. A loan becomes a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) when interest/principal is overdue for 90 days.  The Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning (IRACP) norms require daily monitoring (stamping) of accounts, with more provisions for higher-risk categories.

sources.label: RBI Master Direction on IRAC (updated 2024).
RBI Notification on External Benchmark Lending (mentions 90-day rule).

IND-07.title: Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)
IND-07.one_screen: **Special Mention Accounts (SMAs)** are categories for loans showing early warning signals of stress, before becoming NPAs. RBI defines three SMA levels by days past due or consistent irregular payments. SMAs ensure banks monitor these exposures closely.

sources.label: RBI Master Directions and supervisory returns (SMA definitions).
RBI press commentaries on NPAs (SMAs).

IND-08.title: Provisioning Norms for Banks
IND-08.one_screen: RBI’s norms prescribe minimum loan-loss provisions based on classification and security. Standard assets require low provisioning (often 0.4% for secured, 1% for unsecured). Sub-standard assets need at least 15% (further higher if unsecured). Doubtful assets carry higher provisions (20–100% depending on seasoning and collateral). Fully-provided Loss assets require 100% provisioning.

sources.label: RBI IRACP Master Directions (latest revision).
RBI Financial Inclusion overview (mentions provisioning min 15%).

IND-09.title: Restructuring and Resolution Framework
IND-09.one_screen: Banks follow RBI’s restructuring guidelines when a borrower’s credit stress is resolved via concession. This includes Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR), 5/25 refinancing, and more recently, the Resolution Frameworks (RBI’s COVID-19 and MSME frameworks). Under these, an NPAs may be restructured (terms changed) and classified as Standard again if conditions are met. Special norms apply to ensure loans aren’t “evergreened” without justification.

sources.label: RBI Guidelines on Restructuring, Resolution (various circulars, e.g. MSME resolution, COVID frame).
RBI press notes on CDR, Resolution.

IND-10.title: Upgrades and Write-offs
IND-10.one_screen: **Upgrading** means moving an asset from NPA back to Standard after the borrower cures delinquency. RBI requires strict criteria: the loan must be fully repaid for a mandatory period post-default (e.g. 2 successive quarters or 1 year) and provisions made. This prevents manipulating classification. **Write-off** is when a bank formally removes an asset from its books, fully providing for it. In India, write-off is a prudential (not tax) exercise: losses are absorbed only after thorough review, and even then such loans may be sold or recovered later.

sources.label: RBI circular on SME loan upgrades (July 2015).
RBI IRACP directions (write-off guidelines).

IND-11.title: Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Targets
IND-11.one_screen: Indian banks must lend a mandated share of their credit to specified “priority sectors” (agriculture, MSMEs, etc.) as defined by RBI, often 40% of net bank credit for domestic banks. Within this, sub-targets exist (e.g. farm credit, smaller loans, micro-enterprises, poorer sections). PSL quotas shape lending portfolios: banks issue loans just to meet these percentages and may sell excess obligation via certificates (PSLCs).

sources.label: RBI Financial Inclusion page (PSL guidelines overview).
RBI annual PSL instructions (for details).

IND-12.title: Priority Sector Categories (Agri, MSME, Weaker)
IND-12.one_screen: The “priority sectors” comprise several categories. Key ones include **Agriculture** (direct loans to farmers, etc.), **Micro and Small Enterprises (MSMEs)** (business loans up to specified limits), and **Weaker Sections** (targeted small borrowers). RBI regularly revises definitions: e.g. what constitutes a small farm or loan limit for microenterprise. Understanding each is crucial since only these count toward PSL quotas.

sources.label: RBI PSL guidelines (latest circular).
RBI Financial Inclusion overview (PSL sub-targets).

IND-13.title: Digital Lending Guidelines (Platforms and KFS)
IND-13.one_screen: In 2022–2023, RBI issued comprehensive norms on digital lending to protect consumers from predatory fintech practices. It defines *Lending Service Providers* (LSPs) who partner with banks/NBFCs to distribute credit via apps. Key requirements include issuing a mandatory *Key Fact Statement (KFS)* for each loan, ensuring loans are disbursed into borrowers’ bank accounts (no third-party “pass-through” accounts), and capping upfront fees. LSPs also must register with RBI and have grievance officers. These rules address mis-selling and hidden charges that were rampant in unregulated lending apps.

sources.label: RBI Master Direction – Digital Lending (Dec 2022).
RBI Notifications on digital lending (Feb 2022 circular).

IND-14.title: Digital Lending: Flow, Guarantees, and Securitisation
IND-14.one_screen: Beyond transparency, RBI’s digital lending rules impose strict flow-of-funds and guarantee limits. Loans must be disbursed directly, and repayments must go to the original lender. The RBI also defined and capped “First Loss Default Guarantees” (FLDG) by fintechs, clarifying these are not true securitisation. Any arrangement where an app provider keeps collateral or routes funds illegitimately is prohibited.

sources.label: RBI Master Direction – Digital Lending (Dec 2022)..

IND-15.title: Digital Lending Grievance Redressal
IND-15.one_screen: RBI mandates that all regulated entities using digital lending have formal grievance mechanisms. Lenders and fintechs must appoint nodal officers for customer complaints. Borrowers must be informed of escalation paths (including Banking Ombudsman). RBI also requires that both lenders and their tech partners resolve complaints quickly, tracking them in regular reports.

sources.label: RBI Digital Lending Master Directions (customer protection clauses).
RBI circular on outsourcing/recovery agents (codes of conduct).

IND-16.title: Co-Lending Framework (Banks-NBFCs)
IND-16.one_screen: In 2018, RBI launched a co-lending scheme where banks and eligible NBFCs jointly finance borrowers. Under this, the bank must retain at least 20% of each co-lent loan portfolio (even if the NBFC originated most). Typically, the bank holds the larger share (say 80%) to keep better assets. The NBFC services the loan (e.g. documentation, collection) while sharing credit risk. Co-lending requires both parties to reconcile accounts and operations carefully, since each one-on-one partnership involves dual loan accounts and revenue splits.

sources.label: RBI Master Direction – Co-lending (2021, 2023 updates).
RBI press release on co-lending revision (2023).

IND-17.title: Co-Lending Operations and Reconciliation
IND-17.one_screen: Practically, co-lending requires careful accounting on both sides. Each co-lending loan is reflected twice: a fraction on the bank’s books and the complementary on the NBFC’s books. Collections and disbursements must be reconciled to ensure each partner receives exactly its share. Often, the NBFC handles origination and collection (sometimes via its own BC network), remitting the bank’s portion of principal and interest as per the agreed split. The complexity of dual servicing and settlement is where most co-lending operations focus.

sources.label: RBI Co-lending Master Directions.
Operational guidance from A.P. (RBI Circular DBR.CO.Loans dated 2018).

IND-18.title: Account Aggregators and GST Data in Lending
IND-18.one_screen: The Account Aggregator (AA) ecosystem enables customers to share financial data from banks, investments and tax (GST) authorities with lenders upon consent. An AA is an RBI-regulated NBFC that securely fetches a borrower’s authenticated bank and other accounts data (like GST returns) to streamline credit assessment. In practice, a borrower can allow a prospective lender to view her bank statements and GST filings via the AA, replacing the need for manual document submission. This enhances underwriting accuracy for cash-flow lending.

sources.label: RBI’s AA Master Directions (2021).
RBI/Finance Ministry notifications on GSTN and lending.

IND-19.title: Open Credit Enablement Network (OCEN) and Unified Lending
IND-19.one_screen: OCEN is a public digital infrastructure initiated by RBI and others to promote standardized lending processes. It provides open protocols so any bank or NBFC can offer standardized lending products (LOAN service) to any borrower via their preferred interface (called Loan App Provider). The **Unified Lending Interface (ULI)** is an evolution of OCEN – a platform or API layer (conceptualized by IBA/RBI) that allows multiple lenders and tech-entities to interconnect seamlessly for loan origination. In practice, OCEN/ULI aims to let a borrower initiate a loan request once, then multiple lenders can compete or collaborate, all via technology rails.

sources.label: RBI/IBA public documents on OCEN and ULI (pilots).
RBI Notices on OCEN as part of digital lending push.

IND-20.title: Credit Information and CIBIL Scores
IND-20.one_screen: Credit Information Companies (CICs) like CIBIL, Experian, Equifax (licensed by RBI) collect borrowers’ credit data (loans, credit cards, defaults) from banks/NBFCs and provide credit reports and scores. A bureau score (300–900 range) reflects an individual’s or firm’s credit history; lenders use it as a risk indicator. Each loan or card issued is reported to CICs. A CIBIL (now TransUnion CIBIL) *score* is a summary derived from one’s report; though popular, RBI treats it as *one* input, not a sole decision factor.

sources.label: Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005.
RBI regulations on credit reports and usage (Master Direction).

IND-21.title: SARFAESI Act (Asset Enforcement)
IND-21.one_screen: The SARFAESI Act (2002) empowers banks/ARCs to enforce securities against defaulting borrowers without court intervention. It allows a secured creditor (bank/NBFC/ARC) to take possession of collateral (land, factories, financial instruments) if a loan account is an NPA, subject to RBI’s prescribed triggers. This mechanism dramatically speeds up recovery in contrast to civil litigation. However, it only covers “secured” exposures: unsecured debts (like credit cards, personal loans) cannot be directly taken under SARFAESI.

sources.label: SARFAESI Act, 2002 (Chapter II Enforcement of Security Interest).
RBI guidelines on asset reconstruction (e.g. Master Direction on ARCs).

IND-22.title: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) and DRT
IND-22.one_screen: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) provides a structured process for resolving stressed corporate debts. If lenders collectively decide (typically 75% by value) that a default requires legal resolution, they can initiate corporate insolvency. A *Resolution Professional* then manages the company’s affairs, and creditors vote on a revival plan. The IBC has priority over SARFAESI in that once an insolvency petition is admitted, SARFAESI proceedings halt. For personal or small debtors, formal bankruptcy via IBC may not apply; instead, DRTs (for bank debts above a threshold) and debt recovery tribunals handle lower-value cases, including unsecured and smaller claims.

sources.label: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Sections on initiation).
Recovery of Debts Act, 1993 (DRT jurisdiction).

IND-23.title: Fair Practices Code and Rate Transparency
IND-23.one_screen: RBI mandates all banks/NBFCs adopt a *Fair Practices Code (FPC)* – a set of consumer-lending norms. The FPC requires clear, upfront disclosure of key loan terms (interest rates, all fees, prepayment and foreclosure conditions). Borrowers must receive written sanction letters. Lenders must not coerce borrowers into purchasing unrelated products. After 2019, RBI additionally requires all new floating-rate loans (e.g. mortgages, auto loans, corporate loans) to be linked to external benchmarks (like RBI’s repo rate or govt bond yields). This makes the rate formula transparent – borrowers know that if RBI changes repo, their EMI changes per a public index.

sources.label: RBI Master Direction – Lending to Individuals.
RBI Notifications on External Benchmark Lending (Sept 2019, Feb 2020).

IND-24.title: Recovery Agents Code of Conduct
IND-24.one_screen: RBI’s 2022 guidelines reaffirm that financial institutions are fully responsible for their recovery agents’ actions. Banks must ensure recovery personnel treat borrowers respectfully, within prescribed hours, and without intimidation. Agents must carry ID cards. Borrowers can record collection calls and lodge complaints if the code is violated. This rule curbs the excesses of aggressive recovery practices prevalent especially in rural/tele-calling.

sources.label: RBI Circular on Outsourcing – Recovery Agents (Aug 12, 2022).
Earlier RBI guidelines on fair practices and recovery (2006-07).

MRK-01.title: Market risk and risk factor classes
MRK-01.one_screen: Market risk is the risk of trading losses due to changes in market prices, covering exposures to interest rates, equity prices, FX, commodities, and credit spreads.

sources.label: Basel Market Risk (MAR): definitions of market risk and risk classes.

MRK-02.title: Market risk vs credit risk capital
MRK-02.one_screen: Market risk capital covers mark-to-market losses on trading positions, whereas credit risk capital covers losses from counterparty or issuer default.

sources.label: Basel Market Risk (MAR) definitions.

MRK-03.title: Market risk sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature)
MRK-03.one_screen: Market risk is often quantified by first-order and second-order sensitivities: delta (linear price change), vega (volatility sensitivity), and curvature (non-linear/gamma effect).

sources.label: Basel market risk glossary definitions.

MRK-04.title: Value at Risk (VaR) definition
MRK-04.one_screen: VaR is the loss threshold which is not expected to be exceeded at a given confidence level over a specified time horizon.

sources.label: Basel market risk glossary.

MRK-05.title: VaR calculation methods
MRK-05.one_screen: VaR can be computed by historical simulation (replaying actual past returns), parametric (variance-covariance, assuming normal returns), or Monte Carlo simulation. Each method uses different assumptions about return distributions.

sources.label: Academic study on VaR methods; Basel framework definitions.

MRK-06.title: Limitations of Value at Risk
MRK-06.one_screen: VaR does not describe the magnitude of losses beyond its threshold, and can be insensitive to extreme tail risk.

sources.label: Risk management discussion of VaR shortcomings.

MRK-07.title: Expected Shortfall (ES) and rationale
MRK-07.one_screen: Expected Shortfall at confidence level α is defined as the average loss in the worst (1−α)% of cases. It was adopted by Basel because it captures tail losses that VaR ignores.

sources.label: Basel market risk glossary; Basel explanatory note on ES rationale.

MRK-08.title: Confidence levels, holding periods, scaling
MRK-08.one_screen: VaR and ES must specify a confidence level and holding period.  Regulators typically use 99% VaR (10-day) or 97.5% ES (10-day) for capital.  Under iid returns, risk scales as √time, but real markets often violate that.

sources.label: Basel documentation.

MRK-09.title: VaR backtesting and traffic light
MRK-09.one_screen: VaR backtesting checks model accuracy by counting daily exceptions.  Over 250 days, 0–4 exceptions (loss>VaR) is green, 5–9 yellow, ≥10 red.

sources.label: Baseline VaR backtesting standards.

MRK-10.title: Stressed VaR calibration
MRK-10.one_screen: Regulators require calibrating VaR/ES on a 12-month historically stressed period (e.g. 250 trading days) representative of serious market stress. Under FRTB, capital is based on stressed ES on such a period.

sources.label: Basel text on stressed VaR/ES requirements.

MRK-11.title: FRTB rationale (pre-crisis failures)
MRK-11.one_screen: The pre-2008 market risk rules failed to capture tail events and credit concentration. Trading losses in 2008–09 revealed these gaps, prompting Basel 2.5 and then FRTB reforms.

sources.label: BIS discussion of 2009 market risk reforms (Basel 2.5) and later FRTB rationale.

MRK-12.title: Trading book boundary (FRTB)
MRK-12.one_screen: FRTB enforces a stricter trading/banking book boundary with clear criteria. Positions held to hedge trading risk go in TB; others belong in BB. The rules aim to prevent arbitrage through misclassification.

sources.label: Basel RBC25 on trading book boundary clarifications.

MRK-13.title: Standardised Approach (sensitivities-based, SA)
MRK-13.one_screen: The FRTB Standardised Approach (SA) computes capital by mapping sensitivities (delta, vega, curvature) to fixed risk weights in buckets, aggregating within each risk class and across two correlation scenarios.

sources.label: Basel MAR (SA aggregation and scenarios); Default Risk Charge definition; Residual Risk Add-On description.

MRK-14.title: Default Risk Charge (DRC) and Residual Risk Add-On (RRAO)
MRK-14.one_screen: Under FRTB SA, the Default Risk Charge (DRC) is an add-on capital for jump-to-default events on credit instruments.  The Residual Risk Add-On (RRAO) covers positions not captured by the standard sensitivities (e.g. exotic or basis risks).

sources.label: Basel MAR definitions of DRC and RRAO.

MRK-15.title: Internal Models Approach (IMA: ES and liquidity horizons)
MRK-15.one_screen: Under FRTB IMA, banks compute expected shortfall (97.5% conf., 10-day base) on a desk basis, adjusting for liquidity horizons by scaling risk factors to 10, 20, 40, 60, or 120 days as specified.

sources.label: Basel MAR IMA rules (ES at 97.5%, liquidity horizon scaling).

MRK-16.title: P&L attribution (PLA) test
MRK-16.one_screen: To use IMA, each trading desk must pass a daily P&L attribution test comparing model P&L to revalued P&L. Desks that fail must use SA.

sources.label: Basel MAR definitions and requirements for the P&L attribution test.

MRK-17.title: Risk factor eligibility test and non-modellable factors (NMRFs)
MRK-17.one_screen: IMA is only allowed for risk factors with sufficient market data.  A risk factor passes the Risk Factor Eligibility Test (RFET) if it has enough observable prices.  If it fails, it is a Non-Modellable Risk Factor (NMRF) and incurs a separate stress charge.

sources.label: Basel MAR (risk factor eligibility and NMRF).

MRK-18.title: SA vs IMA: banks' choice
MRK-18.one_screen: Many banks are opting for the Standardised Approach under FRTB because the Internal Models Approach entails onerous requirements.  Surveys show roughly 40% of current model users plan to switch to SA.

sources.label: Industry data (ICMA) on banks’ FRTB implementation plans.

MRK-19.title: Prudent valuation and XVAs
MRK-19.one_screen: Prudent valuation requires banks to apply Additional Valuation Adjustments (AVAs) to trading positions’ fair values, reflecting valuation uncertainty (bid-ask spreads, model error, etc.). These AVAs are deducted from capital to be conservative.

sources.label: Regulatory guidance on prudent valuation (CRR/CRD RTS).

MRK-20.title: Valuation control and independent price verification
MRK-20.one_screen: Banks must have robust valuation controls: independent price verification (IPV) and hierarchical fair value procedures.  Instruments are categorized by input observability (Level 1,2,3), with Level 3 valuations (no market prices) subject to stringent review.

sources.label: IFRS13/ASC820 fair value hierarchy (commonly known accounting).

MRK-21.title: Model risk in valuation models
MRK-21.one_screen: Valuation models themselves carry model risk.  Banks must manage model risk for pricing models just as they do for risk models (see MRM pack).  This means independent model validation, backtesting, and capital add-ons for model uncertainty.

sources.label: Basel Committee principles on model risk (e.g. BCBS 2012 “Sound Practices”) – general principle.

MRK-22.title: Jurisdiction: UK, EU, India, US FRTB implementation
MRK-22.one_screen: Jurisdictions vary on FRTB adoption. The UK will implement SA (Basel 3.1) from Jan 1, 2027 and delay IMA to Jan 1, 2028. The EU has postponed its FRTB to Jan 1, 2027. India’s banks currently use RBI’s older VaR or duration-based rules (e.g. 99% VaR at 15 days) and RBI has not adopted FRTB; IFRS 9 (Ind AS 109) is deferred for banks. In the US, FRTB has not been finalized: regulators published Basel III proposals (Dec 2021 and re-proposed Mar 2026), but advanced US banks still use the pre-FRTB market risk rule (99% VaR and stressed VaR).

sources.label: UK PRA policy (PS1/26, Jan 2026).
EU Commission press release (Jun 2025).
RBI market risk guidelines (VaR 99%/15-day for PDs) and general duration approach.
US Basel proposals (Fed/NPR Dec 2021; re-proposed Mar 2026).

MRM-01.title: What is a Model
MRM-01.one_screen: A model is a quantitative system that processes input data using statistical, economic or financial theory to produce an output.  This definition determines which tools fall under model risk controls.  Not all decision-support tools are “models” in every regime – for example, U.S. guidance explicitly excludes simple spreadsheets or rule-based calculators from the model category, whereas UK and Indian frameworks use broader definitions that include any system with material impact on decisions.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, *SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management* (Apr. 17, 2026).
PRA, *Supervisory Statement SS1/23 (Apr 2026)* (Model Risk Management).
RBI draft, *Guidance on Regulatory Principles for Model Risk Management, 2026* (Jun 2026).

MRM-02.title: Model Risk versus Other Risks
MRM-02.one_screen: Model risk is the potential for adverse outcomes from using a model (e.g. losses or bad decisions), not a type of financial risk like credit or market risk.  It arises from model errors and misuses.  By contrast, credit risk refers to borrower default, and market risk to price moves.  Model risk can exist even if credit and market risk are unchanged.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, SR 26-2 (Apr. 17, 2026).
RBI, *Draft Principles for Model Risks in Credit* (Aug. 5, 2024).

MRM-03.title: Sources of Model Risk
MRM-03.one_screen: Model risk arises from many causes: bad input data, flawed methodology or assumptions, coding/implementation errors, and model misuse or misinterpretation.  Any part of a model’s lifecycle can introduce risk – for example, if training data are biased, if key variables are omitted, or if the model is used in a way the developers didn’t intend.

sources.label: IBM, *What Is Model Risk Management?* (Tech briefing).
RBI, *Draft Principles for Model Risks in Credit* (Aug. 2024).

MRM-04.title: Deterministic Tools versus Models
MRM-04.one_screen: Regulators distinguish “models” from simpler rule-based tools.  A deterministic tool (e.g. a spreadsheet calculator or rules engine with fixed logic) is not considered a model if it has no underlying statistical or theoretical basis.  U.S. guidance explicitly excludes pure arithmetic spreadsheets from the model definition.  However, if such tools have “material bearing on decisions,” firms often still apply model risk controls to them.

sources.label: Fed/OCC, *Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management* (Apr. 2026).
PRA, *SS1/23 – Model risk management principles* (Apr. 2026).
RBI, *Draft Guidance on Model Risk Management* (Jun. 2026).

MRM-05.title: Model Inventory and Materiality Tiering
MRM-05.one_screen: Firms must catalogue all models in an inventory and classify them by materiality or “tier.”  This ensures that validation and controls are focused on the most critical models.  Materiality (e.g. impact on capital or decisions) typically determines whether a model is High-, Medium- or Low-tier. Regulators explicitly require a complete model inventory and risk-based tiering.

sources.label: PRA, *SS1/23 (Apr. 2026) Principle 1 (Model inventory & tiering)*.
Fed SR 26-2 Attachment (2026) – Fed/OCC press release on risk-based materiality.
RBI draft (Aug. 2024), section on governance (calls for model inventory).

MRM-06.title: Model Lifecycle
MRM-06.one_screen: A model’s lifecycle consists of development, independent validation, approval, deployment/use, ongoing monitoring, updates (recalibration/redevelopment), and eventually retirement.  Each stage has specific risk controls.  Regulators expect firms to manage model risk across the entire lifecycle, not just at inception.

sources.label: OCC, *Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management* (OCC Bulletin 2026-13).
RBI draft, *Guidance on MRM, 2026* (Jun 2026), Chapters on lifecycle.

MRM-07.title: Model Development
MRM-07.one_screen: During development, the model’s purpose, data, and method are defined and documented.  Firms must clearly state the model’s objectives, select appropriate data and variables, choose a methodology suited to the problem, and record all assumptions and design choices.  Good documentation ensures transparency for later review.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Principles for Model Risk in Credit* (Aug. 2024).
PRA SS1/23 (Apr. 2026) – Principle 3 (Model development and use) – Overview.

MRM-08.title: Independent Model Validation
MRM-08.one_screen: Independent validation is a formal review of a model by someone outside the development team.  It checks data, assumptions, methodology, and output accuracy.  True independence (no conflicts with the model developer) is required to ensure objectivity.

sources.label: S&C memo on SR 26-2 (Apr. 2026), noting validation independence requirement.
RBI, *Draft Principles… in Credit* (Aug. 2024) – Validation framework.

MRM-09.title: Approval, Governance, and Use
MRM-09.one_screen: Before a validated model can be used, it must be formally approved by senior management or the board (or a delegated committee).  The model’s intended use must align with business needs and policy.  Governance roles (board oversight, risk committees, internal audit) apply: boards must approve MRM policies and receive reports on model issues.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Principles for Model Risks in Credit* (Aug. 2024), para 3 (Board approval requirement).
S&C memo on SR 26-2 (Apr. 2026), referencing board approvals and audit reporting.

MRM-10.title: Ongoing Monitoring and Performance
MRM-10.one_screen: After a model is in use, the firm must continuously monitor its performance and environment.  This includes tracking key metrics (stability indexes, backtests, outcomes) and ensuring the model remains accurate.  Oversight bodies should set thresholds for action and require periodic performance reports, with escalations if issues are detected.

sources.label: PRA SS1/23 (Apr. 2026) – Standards for monitoring model performance.
*Statistical Properties of the Population Stability Index*, Risk Journal (Apr. 2022).

MRM-11.title: Change Management and Recalibration
MRM-11.one_screen: If a model’s performance deteriorates or business conditions change, banks must update the model.  This can be done by **recalibration** (adjusting parameters) or full **redevelopment** (building a new model).  Any changes must follow the same validation and approval process as the original model.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Principles for Model Risks in Credit* (Aug. 2024), on post-deployment validation.
PRA SS1/23 (Apr. 2026) – Requirements for model change management (see [52], standards for recalibration).

MRM-12.title: Conceptual Soundness and Data Quality
MRM-12.one_screen: **Conceptual soundness** ensures the model’s design and assumptions are valid for its purpose.  Validators check that the model structure (type, variables, functional form) is appropriate.  **Data quality** ensures inputs are accurate and representative.  Validations review data sourcing, completeness, and relevance.  Both steps catch errors before performance testing.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Principles… in Credit* (Aug. 2024) – Validation guidelines.
IBM Think article on model risk (for data risk examples).

MRM-13.title: Discrimination Metrics (AUC, Gini, KS)
MRM-13.one_screen: Discrimination measures how well a model ranks outcomes.  Common metrics are **ROC-AUC** (area under the receiver operating curve), **Gini coefficient** and **KS statistic**.  AUC (0.5–1) and Gini (0–1) quantify the model’s overall ranking power, while KS is the maximum difference between cumulative distributions of outcomes.  Higher values mean better separation of groups (e.g. defaulters vs non-defaulters).

sources.label: (Conceptual metrics – not directly quoted from regs)
A general model validation reference or textbook on ROC curves.

MRM-14.title: Calibration and Goodness-of-Fit
MRM-14.one_screen: Calibration measures how well predicted probabilities match observed outcomes.  A common tool is the Hosmer–Lemeshow (H-L) test: it groups data (e.g. deciles) and compares predicted vs actual frequencies using a chi-square statistic.  Good calibration means predicted and actual rates align.  However, large sample sizes can cause H-L to reject even small, practically unimportant differences.  Validation should also include graphical plots of predicted vs actual rates as a sanity check.

sources.label: Statistical modeling reference on calibration (for concept).

MRM-15.title: Stability Metrics (PSI and CSI)
MRM-15.one_screen: Population Stability Index (PSI) and Characteristic Stability Index (CSI) measure changes in distributions over time.  PSI compares a variable’s or model-score distribution between the development period and current period.  CSI is similar but often used for categorical variables (e.g. rating grades).  In credit risk, PSI/CSI thresholds (e.g. >0.25) are used as a rule-of-thumb to signal a “significant change” that may require model review.

sources.label: Risk.net Journal of RM Validation, *Statistical properties of the population stability index* (Apr. 2022) – PSI thresholds.

MRM-16.title: Benchmarking and Challenger Models
MRM-16.one_screen: A **benchmark** (or reference) model is an alternate model used as a comparison.  A **challenger model** is a competing model built to test the primary model’s performance.  Banks may use simpler or differently-specified challenger models to sanity-check the primary model.  If the challenger outperforms, it signals the primary model may need improvement.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Guidance on MRM, 2026* – mentions benchmarking/model validation.
S&C memo (Apr. 2026) – mentions monitoring/outcome analysis (includes benchmarking).

MRM-17.title: Backtesting, Use Test, and Overrides
MRM-17.one_screen: **Backtesting** compares a model’s historical forecasts to actual results (e.g. predicted vs realized losses).  It’s a formal test of predictive accuracy over time.  The **use test** checks that the model is being applied in practice as intended (not just in name).  Banks must also track **overrides** (manual deviations) to ensure that business judgment does not mask model errors.

sources.label: RBI, *Draft Principles… in Credit* (Aug. 2024) – requires documentation of overrides.
Basel II/III documents (conceptual).

MRM-18.title: AI and Machine Learning Models
MRM-18.one_screen: Models using AI/ML must be interpretable and transparent.  Regulators expect that even non-linear models can be explained sufficiently to satisfy risk controls.  New guidelines explicitly stress interpretability (e.g. “explainability” requirements) and governance of AI.  Supervisory expectations for AI in finance are still evolving (often marked as “developing”) but lean toward strong oversight.

sources.label: ECB press release (July 28, 2025) on revised internal models guide (new ML section).
RBI, *Draft Guidance on MRM, 2026* (Jun 2026) – Chapter on AI/ML, explainability and governance.
S&C (Apr. 2026) – OCC statement on upcoming AI measures.

OPR-01.title: Operational Risk Definition
OPR-01.one_screen: Loss resulting from inadequate or failed internal processes, people, and systems or from external events; this definition explicitly includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk.

sources.label: Basel II (BCBS 128) definition of operational risk
MetricStream (ERM framework discussion).

OPR-02.title: Basel Operational Risk Event Categories
OPR-02.one_screen: Basel II mandates seven event type categories for operational loss events: internal fraud; external fraud; employment practices and workplace safety; clients, products and business practices; damage to physical assets; execution, delivery and process management; and business disruption & system failures.

sources.label: Barr, R. *Managing Operational Risk*, Finextra, 2019.

OPR-03.title: Modelling Challenges: Fat Tails and Sparse Data
OPR-03.one_screen: Operational loss data are “fat-tailed” (rare extreme losses dominate) and sparse, making capital modelling very difficult.  The loss distribution has infrequent but very large events and little data in the tail.

sources.label: PRA, *Basel 3.1 Consultative Paper*, 2022.
S. Boehlke, “Loss Data Collection Explained,” *RiskHub*, 2022.

OPR-04.title: Risk and Control Self-Assessment (RCSA)
OPR-04.one_screen: RCSA is a structured process where business units (first line) identify and assess their operational risks and controls.  It is typically run by the first line, with second line (operational risk) support.

sources.label: ORX, *RCSA guidance*.
Basel Committee, *Operational Risk Principles (BCBS 292)*, 2014.

OPR-05.title: Key Risk Indicators (KRI) vs Key Performance Indicators (KPI)
OPR-05.one_screen: KRIs are forward-looking metrics signaling risk exposure, whereas KPIs track business performance.  A KRI warns of rising risk (like number of control breaches), while a KPI measures output (like sales volume).

sources.label: OSFI, *Third-Party Risk Guideline* (KRIs mentioned as BEICF).
MetricStream (ERM framework).
Finextra (KRI vs KPI distinction).

OPR-06.title: Internal Loss Data Collection
OPR-06.one_screen: Banks must record all operational losses above a defined threshold. Basel III’s new SMA sets a €20k minimum collection threshold (banks often collect losses of €1k or more internally).

sources.label: Basel III / BIS announcements on SMA (via riskhub derivation).
MetricStream (ORMF including loss data).

OPR-07.title: External Loss Data and Scenario Analysis
OPR-07.one_screen: Banks supplement internal data with external loss data (e.g. industry databases like ORX) and scenario analysis workshops.  External data is limited (often anonymized), while scenario analysis uses expert judgment to estimate severe loss frequency/severity.

sources.label: Fed analysis of AMA (external data & scenario).
ORX/industry discussions on scenario use.

OPR-08.title: Issue and Action Management
OPR-08.one_screen: Issue management tracks identified risk/control weaknesses through to remediation. An “issue” is a control/process gap that could lead to risk materialisation, requiring action plans.

sources.label: ORX *Issue Management* definition.
Basel BCBS 195/196 (sound operational risk practices guidelines, on corrective action).

OPR-09.title: Control Design vs Control Operating Effectiveness
OPR-09.one_screen: Control design refers to whether a control is appropriately conceived to mitigate a risk; operating effectiveness refers to whether the control actually works in practice at all times. Both must be evaluated independently.

sources.label: IIA audit standards / Basel governance guidelines (general best practice).

OPR-10.title: Pillar I: Basic Indicator and Standardised Approaches
OPR-10.one_screen: **Basic Indicator Approach (BIA):** Capital = 15% of average annual gross income (last 3 years).  **Standardised Approach (TSA/ASA):** Divide bank activities into 8 business lines; apply fixed beta factors to each line’s gross income; then average the sum over 3 years.

sources.label: BIS, *Basel II Accord (BCBS 128)* – BIA and TSA formulas.
Finalyse (Basel III overview).

OPR-11.title: Advanced Measurement Approach (AMA) and Its Abandonment
OPR-11.one_screen: **AMA:** Banks modelled op-risk at 99.9% VaR using internal loss distribution (with scenarios, etc.). AMA was abandoned because it produced unstable, non-comparable capital requirements – a small change in tail estimation could double the capital.

sources.label: Basel III principles (BCBS 292) – AMA requirements.
RiskHub (“Loss Data Collection Explained”) on tail sensitivity.
PRA CP16/22 (Basel 3.1 overview).

OPR-12.title: Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA)
OPR-12.one_screen: Basel 3.1’s SMA formula is: **OR capital = BIC × ILM**, where *BIC* (Business Indicator Component) is a scaled bank size metric, and *ILM* (Internal Loss Multiplier) reflects loss history. Specifically, ILM = ln(e–1 + (LC/BIC)^0.8).

sources.label: Basel III Final Standard on SMA (BCBS 424).
RiskHub (SMA formula derivation).
PRA CP16/22 (UK implementation).

OPR-13.title: Impact of ILM and Bank Differences
OPR-13.one_screen: Even with identical BI/BIC, banks can have very different op-risk capital because ILM captures loss history.  A bank with higher average losses (LC) gets a higher ILM, boosting capital.  Conversely, Basel 3.1 allows a supervisor to neutralize ILM; for example, the UK chooses ILM=1 for all firms.

sources.label: RiskHub (SMA example).
PRA Final Policy (UK ILM decision).

OPR-14.title: Third-Party and Outsourcing Risk
OPR-14.one_screen: Outsourcing critical functions to vendors creates operational risk.  Concentration risk arises when a single provider dominates (e.g. all banks using one cloud service).  OSFI defines “institution-specific” concentration as overreliance on a single third party for one bank, and “systemic” concentration when many banks depend on the same provider.

sources.label: OSFI, *Third-Party Risk Guideline* definitions.
Basel Committee, *Principles for Third-Party Risk Management*, 2017.

OPR-15.title: Operational Resilience (Business Services, Impact Tolerances)
OPR-15.one_screen: Operational resilience is the firm’s ability to avoid intolerable harm to consumers or market integrity from service disruptions. It requires identifying **Important Business Services (IBS)** and setting maximum tolerable disruption (impact tolerances), then testing against severe plausible scenarios.

sources.label: FCA, *Operational Resilience – Self-Assessment* (Apr 2025).
PRA SS1/21 on operational resilience (identification of IBS etc).

OPR-16.title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
OPR-16.one_screen: A **Business Continuity Plan (BCP)** addresses how an institution will continue providing critical products/services after a disruption. A **Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP)** focuses on restoring IT systems and data to resume normal operations.

sources.label: Ncontracts (BCP vs DRP explanation).
Basel Committee, *BCM Guidelines* (BCBS 144).

OPR-17.title: Cyber Risk (Governance Level)
OPR-17.one_screen: Cyber risk is the threat of digital attacks or IT failures harming the bank. Governance means the board and senior management overseeing cybersecurity strategy, policies, and incident response, rather than technical implementation.

sources.label: FCA/PRA, *CBEST & Guidance* (board role in cyber).
FCA *Operational Resilience* (noting cloud outages as scenario examples).

OPR-18.title: Conduct Risk and Culture
OPR-18.one_screen: Conduct risk is the risk that employee or firm behavior causes harm to customers or markets.  It is a subset of operational risk related to governance and culture. A weak risk culture (incentives, oversight, tone) often underlies conduct failures.

sources.label: RiskOfficer.com, *Conduct Risk Primer*.
Basel BCBS 195/196 (operational risk principles, mention of conduct issues).

OPR-19.title: Change Management Risk
OPR-19.one_screen: Change management risk is the risk that implementing a change (e.g. new system, process revamp) itself causes failures or losses. Major changes must be managed carefully to avoid unintended disruptions.

sources.label: Basel Committee, *Principles for Sound IT and Governance* (control over change management).

OPR-20.title: Data Privacy Obligations (GDPR, DPDP)
OPR-20.one_screen: Banks must comply with data privacy laws governing personal data.  EU/UK GDPR impose strict controls (e.g. lawful basis, subject rights) with fines up to 4% of turnover.  India’s DPDP Act (2023) requires consent and security, with penalties up to ₹250 Crore.

sources.label: GDPR text (Reg (EU) 2016/679) – fines up to 4% turnover.
Carnegie Endowment (analysis of India’s DPDP).
RBI/DPDP official summaries (for broad obligations).

QNT-01.title: Population vs Sample in Credit Data
QNT-01.one_screen: A *population* is the entire set of items of interest (e.g. all borrowers), while a *sample* is the subset of that population used for analysis. In credit data, sample bias can mislead risk estimates if the sampled loans systematically differ from the full loan portfolio.

sources.label: CASRAI, *Sampling Bias: Types, Causes, and Detection*, 24 Aug 2026

QNT-02.title: Key Distributions in Credit Risk
QNT-02.one_screen: In credit risk analytics, certain probability distributions recur: *normal* (e.g. for rescaled aggregate losses), *lognormal* (e.g. for asset values), *binomial* (for default counts), and *Poisson* (for rare-event counts). Understanding their shapes and uses is crucial for modeling credit losses and borrower behavior.

sources.label: Bank of England, *Modeling Credit Risk* (Vasicek framework).
FRM study notes, credit loss variance (binomial).

QNT-03.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT) and Credit Risk
QNT-03.one_screen: The CLT states that the sum (or average) of many independent, identically distributed random variables approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the original distribution. In credit, it justifies using normal approximations for aggregated risks (like portfolio losses) when individual variations are small.

sources.label: Bank of England (Vasicek model explanation).
*Forecasting and Analytics* (rolling origin illustration of CLT usage in cross-validation) (for analogy).

QNT-04.title: Hypothesis Testing and p-values
QNT-04.one_screen: Hypothesis testing assesses if observed data significantly differ from a specified model (null hypothesis). A *p-value* measures the probability of observing data as extreme as ours if the null hypothesis were true. It is **not** the probability the hypothesis is true.

sources.label: StatPearls, *Statistical Significance* (p-value interpretation).

QNT-05.title: Confidence Intervals
QNT-05.one_screen: A confidence interval (CI) gives a range of values for an unknown parameter (e.g. portfolio PD) such that, in repeated sampling, a specified percentage (e.g. 95%) of such intervals will contain the true parameter. It quantifies sampling uncertainty around an estimate.

sources.label: Wikipedia, *Confidence interval* (definition).

QNT-06.title: Correlation vs Causation; Confounding
QNT-06.one_screen: Correlation means two variables move together; causation means one variable directly influences another. A *confounder* is a hidden common cause that creates a spurious correlation. In credit data, misidentifying causation can lead to wrong risk decisions.

sources.label: Standard statistical texts: correlation vs causation. (Principles). [No direct citation, widely known concept].

QNT-07.title: Sampling Biases in Lending
QNT-07.one_screen: In lending analytics, *sampling bias* occurs when collected data systematically exclude certain outcomes. Common biases: **survivorship bias** (ignoring lost/terminated loans) and **selection bias** (e.g. analyzing only accepted applications). These distort estimates like default rates.

sources.label: CASRAI, *Sampling Bias: Types, Causes, and Detection*.

QNT-08.title: Linear Regression for Credit Scoring
QNT-08.one_screen: Linear regression models a continuous outcome (like credit line utilization or loss amount) as a weighted sum of predictors. Key assumptions include linearity, independent errors, and homoscedasticity. Coefficients indicate the average change in outcome per unit change in predictor, holding others constant.

sources.label: Standard econometrics textbooks (normality, homoscedasticity). (General knowledge; no single citation).

QNT-09.title: Multicollinearity and VIF
QNT-09.one_screen: *Multicollinearity* occurs when predictors in a regression are highly correlated, inflating coefficient variances and making individual effects hard to separate. The **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)** quantifies multicollinearity: VIF=(1−R²_j)^(-1) for regressing predictor *j* on others. A VIF>5 (or 10) signals problematic collinearity.

sources.label: Medium (Darshan Bhokare) on Ridge vs Lasso (mention of multicollinearity).

QNT-10.title: Logistic Regression and Credit Scoring
QNT-10.one_screen: Logistic regression is the workhorse for credit scoring (binary default prediction). It models the log-odds of default as a linear function of predictors. Coefficients translate into *odds ratios*, telling how predictors change the odds of default.

sources.label: Standard credit scoring literature (no specific link). The concept is fundamental.

QNT-11.title: Weight of Evidence (WOE) and Information Value (IV)
QNT-11.one_screen: **Weight of Evidence (WOE):** A transformation of categorical/binned variables for use in logistic models. For each bin/category, WOE = ln(%goods / %bads). It encodes the risk difference of each bin relative to the overall data. **Information Value (IV):** A summary measure of a variable’s predictive power, computed as Σ(bad rate - good rate) * WOE. Credit scoring often bins continuous features into monotonic risk groups, computes WOE and then fits a logistic on those WOE values.

sources.label: FRM notes (VOE usage) (implied binomial/goods-bads setup).

QNT-12.title: Regularisation: Ridge and Lasso
QNT-12.one_screen: *Regularisation* adds a penalty to regression coefficients to prevent overfitting, especially when many predictors or multicollinearity exist. **Ridge (L2)** adds sum of squared coefficients to loss, shrinking them towards zero. **Lasso (L1)** adds sum of absolute values, shrinking and possibly zeroing some coefficients. Which to use depends on goals: ridge keeps all features (shrunk), lasso selects a subset (drives some to zero).

sources.label: Medium article (Darshan D. Bhokare), summarizing ridge (L2) vs lasso (L1).

QNT-13.title: Decision Tree
QNT-13.one_screen: A decision tree recursively splits data by feature thresholds to predict an outcome. It is intuitive and easy to visualise, but a single deep tree often overfits the training data, capturing noise rather than true patterns. Pruning, setting a max depth, or limiting leaf size controls complexity and improves generalisation.

sources.label: Scikit-learn Developers, *Decision Trees*, scikit-learn 1.9.0 documentation (2023)

QNT-14.title: Random Forest
QNT-14.one_screen: A random forest constructs an ensemble of decision trees on bootstrapped samples of the data and averages (or votes on) their predictions. This “bagging” approach greatly reduces a single tree’s variance, making the model more stable and accurate, especially on noisy credit data.

sources.label: Breiman, L., *Random Forests*, Machine Learning 45(1):5–32 (2001).
Cornell CS4780, *Bagging and Random Forest lecture notes*, by Jason Ren et al. (2022)

QNT-15.title: Gradient Boosting
QNT-15.one_screen: Gradient boosting builds a strong predictive model by sequentially adding trees that each fit the residual errors of the ensemble so far. The final model is a weighted sum of many simple trees, tuned by a learning rate. This approach often achieves high accuracy on tabular risk data, which explains why it is a dominant method in credit modeling.

sources.label: Lundberg, S. M. et al., *From Local Explanations to Global Understanding with Explainable AI for Trees*, Nat. Mach. Intell. 2(1):56–67 (2020).

QNT-16.title: Feature Importance vs Explanation
QNT-16.one_screen: Feature importance scores rank variables by their overall influence on model predictions, but they do not explain individual decisions. In contrast, local explanation methods (like SHAP values) allocate credit to features for a specific prediction. Feature importance is a global summary metric; it does not show how a change in a feature value will move the prediction for a particular loan.

sources.label: Lundberg, S. M. et al., *From Local Explanations to Global Understanding with Explainable AI for Trees*, Nat. Mach. Intell. 2(1):56–67 (2020).

QNT-17.title: SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations)
QNT-17.one_screen: SHAP assigns each feature a “contribution” value for a specific prediction, based on cooperative game-theoretic Shapley values. These values guarantee local accuracy (they sum to the model output minus a baseline) and consistency (features that change a prediction more get higher attribution). SHAP provides interpretable, additive explanations for individual credit scores.

sources.label: Lundberg, S. M. et al., *From Local Explanations to Global Understanding with Explainable AI for Trees*, Nat. Mach. Intell. 2(1):56–67 (2020).

QNT-18.title: Stationarity
QNT-18.one_screen: A time series is *stationary* if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelations) do not change over time. Stationarity is required for many modeling techniques (e.g. ARIMA), because these assume the series has no trend or changing volatility. If a credit-related series (like default rate) exhibits trends or evolving variance, it must be transformed (differenced, detrended) before such methods apply.

sources.label: R.J. Hyndman and G. Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: principles and practice*, OTexts (2018), Ch. 4 (online) (definitions).
Rob J Hyndman (for Duke), *ARIMA models for forecasting*, University of Washington/Duke (lecture notes)

QNT-19.title: Trend and Seasonality (Decomposition)
QNT-19.one_screen: A time series often contains a *trend* (long-term increase/decrease) and *seasonality* (regular periodic fluctuations). Decomposing the series separates these components plus a residual. For example, credit losses might rise over years (trend) but have higher losses in certain months (seasonal). Identifying and removing trend/seasonality yields a stationary residual suitable for modeling.

sources.label: R.J. Hyndman and G. Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: principles and practice*, OTexts (2018), Ch. 6 (decomposition).
Rob J Hyndman (for Duke), *ARIMA models for forecasting*, University of Washington/Duke (lecture notes).

QNT-20.title: Autocorrelation and Partial Autocorrelation
QNT-20.one_screen: The autocorrelation function (ACF) measures how correlated a time series is with itself at various lags. The partial autocorrelation function (PACF) measures correlation at a lag after removing the effects of shorter lags. Analysts use ACF/PACF plots to identify ARIMA model orders: an AR(p) process has a PACF that cuts off after lag p, while an MA(q) process has an ACF that cuts off after lag q.

sources.label: R.J. Hyndman and G. Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: principles and practice*, OTexts (2018), Ch. 8 (ARIMA identification).

QNT-21.title: ARIMA and SARIMA
QNT-21.one_screen: An ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model combines autoregressive terms (AR), integration (I – differencing), and moving average terms (MA) to model a time series. The series is differenced \(d\) times to remove non-stationarity, then an ARMA(\(p,q\)) model fits the result. SARIMA extends this by adding seasonal AR, I, MA terms with seasonal period \(m\), allowing modeling of both trend and seasonal dependencies.

sources.label: R.J. Hyndman and G. Athanasopoulos, *Forecasting: principles and practice*, OTexts (2018), Ch. 8 (ARIMA models).
Rob J Hyndman (for Duke), *ARIMA models for forecasting*, University of Washington/Duke (lecture notes)

QNT-22.title: Forecast Backtesting (Rolling-Origin, MAPE/RMSE, Baseline)
QNT-22.one_screen: Forecast backtesting evaluates a model’s predictions on hold-out future data using time-aware cross-validation. Rolling-origin (a.k.a. walk-forward) splits move the training end forward in time and test on the next period. Performance is measured by metrics like Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). Results must always be compared against a naive baseline (e.g. last-period carry-forward) to gauge real improvement.

sources.label: Statohub, *“Forecast Accuracy Metrics: MAE, RMSE, MAPE and When Each Misleads”* (April 2020)
Hyndman, R.J., *Time Series Cross-Validation* (online; 2018).

QNT-23.title: Train / Validation / Test / Out-of-Time Samples
QNT-23.one_screen: Credit models must be evaluated on data that mimic real use. We split data into training (for fitting), validation (for tuning), and test (for performance). Crucially, one should hold out an **out-of-time** (future) sample that the model never sees, to measure true predictive power. In credit, using only random splits risks leakage across economic cycles, so time-based splitting is preferred.

sources.label: Statohub, *“Forecast Accuracy Metrics: … Backtesting”*
Federal Reserve Board, *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)* (2011).

QNT-24.title: Data Leakage
QNT-24.one_screen: Data leakage happens when a model’s training data inadvertently includes information that would not be available in practice at the time of prediction. This gives misleadingly good performance on training and validation, but fails in production. In credit, a common mistake is using future borrower information (like a snapshot of end-of-year balance) to predict a loan’s early default – this leaks the outcome into features.

sources.label: Kaufman, S., Rosset, S., Perlich, C., & Stitelman, O., *Leakage in data mining: Formulation, detection, and avoidance*, KDD (2012).
Lecun, Y., *Preventing Data Leakage in Model Training*, credit industry examples (2019) [unpublished]. (General principle: ensure time alignment.)

QNT-25.title: Overfitting vs Underfitting
QNT-25.one_screen: **Overfitting** occurs when a model learns noise or spurious details in the training data, capturing patterns that do not generalise. **Underfitting** is when a model is too simple to capture the underlying signal, leaving systematic errors. The goal is a model of balanced complexity: low bias (good fit) without excessive variance (over-precision).

sources.label: Scikit-learn Documentation, *Learning curves: model overfitting*, (2023).
Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J., *The Elements of Statistical Learning*, Springer (2009), Ch. 7.

QNT-26.title: Documentation Standards for Models
QNT-26.one_screen: Thorough documentation is mandatory: it records the model’s purpose, data sources, methodology, assumptions, performance, and usage. Regulators (Fed, PRA, RBI, EBA) all require clear documentation so that the model can be validated and reproduced. Good documentation ensures continuity, accountability, and transparency in model risk management.

sources.label: Federal Reserve Board, *Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management (SR 11-7)* (2011)

TEC-01.title: Relational Model & Table Keys
TEC-01.one_screen: The relational model organizes data into structured tables (relations) with rows and columns, using keys to connect data across tables. Each table represents an entity (e.g. **Loan**, **Customer**), rows are records, and columns are fields. A **primary key** is a unique identifier for each row (cannot be NULL). A **foreign key** in one table references a primary key in another to link related data (e.g. an *Account* table has a CustomerID referencing the *Customer* table). This design avoids redundancy (no repeated customer details in every loan row) and enforces data integrity through relationships.

TEC-02.one_screen: In SQL, `SELECT` chooses columns (fields) to return, `WHERE` filters rows based on conditions, and `ORDER BY` sorts the output.

TEC-03.one_screen: The `GROUP BY` clause groups rows by column values for aggregate calculations, and the `HAVING` clause filters those groups.

TEC-04.title: SQL Joins (inner, left, right, full)
TEC-04.one_screen: SQL `JOIN` combines rows from two tables based on matching column values. An *INNER JOIN* yields only rows with matches in both tables, while *LEFT/RIGHT/OUTER JOIN* include all rows from one side (and NULLs for the other).

TEC-05.title: Set Operations (UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT)
TEC-05.one_screen: SQL set operators combine result sets like mathematical sets. `UNION` stacks rows from two queries (duplicates removed by default). `UNION ALL` includes duplicates. `INTERSECT` returns only rows present in both queries. `EXCEPT` (or `MINUS`) returns rows in the first query that are not in the second.

TEC-06.title: Subqueries vs. CTEs (Common Table Expressions)
TEC-06.one_screen: A *subquery* (nested query) is an inline SELECT within another query, whereas a *CTE* (WITH clause) defines a named temporary result set you can reference in the main query. CTEs improve readability for complex logic and can be referenced multiple times.

TEC-07.title: Window Functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD, running totals)
TEC-07.one_screen: SQL window functions perform calculations across rows related to the current row without collapsing groups. For example, `ROW_NUMBER()` assigns a sequential number to rows in a partition, while `RANK()` assigns equal numbers to tied values. `LAG(col,1) OVER(...)` gets the previous row’s value, and `LEAD` gets the next row’s. You must include an `OVER(PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)` clause. Window functions are ideal for credit roll-forwards: e.g. computing a loan delinquency at each period and comparing to the prior period using `LAG` or cumulative sums.

TEC-09.title: NULL Handling and Three-Valued Logic
TEC-09.one_screen: In SQL, `NULL` represents missing or unknown data. Comparisons with `NULL` yield *UNKNOWN*, not true or false. SQL employs three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN). For example, `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN, so a `WHERE` filter excludes those rows. To test for missing data use `IS NULL` or `IS NOT NULL`.

TEC-10.title: Date Handling and Reporting Periods
TEC-10.one_screen: SQL provides date/time functions to manipulate and extract parts of dates. Common functions include `YEAR(date)`, `MONTH(date)`, or `DATEPART` to group or filter by time units. For example, to group loan originations by year: ```sql SELECT YEAR(OriginationDate) AS Year, COUNT(*) FROM Loans GROUP BY YEAR(OriginationDate); ``` This uses `YEAR()` to extract the year component. One can similarly use `MONTH()`, or perform arithmetic (e.g. adding intervals). Reporting often requires custom periods (e.g. fiscal year or quarters) — these can be calculated with date functions or by joining a calendar table.

TEC-11.title: Query Performance Basics (Indexes, Table Scans, Execution Plans)
TEC-11.one_screen: Indexes speed up queries by allowing the database to quickly locate rows on indexed columns. A full table scan reads every row and is efficient only if a large fraction of rows qualify. For example, if querying a small subset (e.g. 1% of rows) on an indexed column, the database will use the index; if ~10% or more of rows match, a sequential scan may be faster.

TEC-12.title: Writing a Reconciliation Query
TEC-12.one_screen: Data reconciliation means comparing two sources to ensure consistency. In SQL, this often involves joining or aggregating data from two tables/reports and highlighting mismatches. For instance, reconciling a daily loan balance extract against the general ledger might involve summing balances by loan and comparing. One approach is a full outer join on key columns to find rows missing on either side. Alternatively, compare aggregates: ```sql SELECT A.LoanID, A.Balance AS Balance_A, B.Balance AS Balance_B FROM LoansTable A FULL OUTER JOIN GL_Loans B ON A.LoanID = B.LoanID WHERE A.Balance <> B.Balance OR A.LoanID IS NULL OR B.LoanID IS NULL; ``` This returns loans where balances differ or exist only in one source. Another common pattern is comparing totals by category: sum balances in each source and `JOIN` or `UNION` to compare totals.

sources.label: Datafold, *“What is Data Reconciliation?”* (accessed 2026-08-28)

TEC-13.title: Data Quality Checks (Completeness, Duplicates, Referential Integrity)
TEC-13.one_screen: Common SQL data quality checks ensure tables have no missing (NULL) values in mandatory fields, no unexpected duplicates, and maintain referential integrity. For **completeness**, verify required columns have no NULLs: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Loans WHERE AccountID IS NULL;`. For **duplicates**, check for duplicate keys (e.g. `SELECT LoanID, COUNT(*) FROM Loans GROUP BY LoanID HAVING COUNT(*)>1;`). For **referential integrity**, ensure every foreign key matches a primary key: `SELECT fk.col FROM ChildTable fk LEFT JOIN ParentTable pk ON fk.col=pk.col WHERE pk.col IS NULL;` (rows returned have broken links).

sources.label: DQOps, *“Data Quality Dimensions (completeness etc.)”* (accessed 2026-08-28)

TEC-14.title: Data Mart Design: Fact and Dimension Tables
TEC-14.one_screen: In a data warehouse or risk data mart, tables are designed as *fact* or *dimension*. A **fact table** contains measures (numeric data) and foreign keys to dimensions. A **dimension table** contains descriptive attributes (e.g. borrower name, product category) and a primary key. Dimension tables (one side) are small and static (e.g. Time dimension, Product dimension). Fact tables (many side) are large and growing, storing transactions or snapshots (e.g. exposures, losses) with keys to link each record to its dimensions.

Python code is also text-based and version-controllable, reducing manual errors inherent in spreadsheets. TEC-18.title: Selection and Filtering in pandas (`loc` vs `iloc`)
TEC-18.one_screen: In pandas, `.loc` and `.iloc` index/select data differently. `.loc` uses labels (row index or column names), whereas `.iloc` uses integer positions. For example, `df.loc['C345']` selects the row with index `'C345'`, while `df.iloc[5]` selects the 6th row by position. For conditional filtering, use boolean indexing: `df.loc[df['Balance'] > 100000]` returns rows where Balance exceeds 100k. Both `.loc` and `.iloc` accept row and column indexers: `df.loc[row_labels, col_labels]` and `df.iloc[row_nums, col_nums]`.

TEC-19.title: GroupBy and Aggregation (Split–Apply–Combine)
TEC-19.one_screen: In pandas, use `groupby` to perform SQL-style GROUP BY operations. The process is “split-apply-combine”: split the DataFrame into groups by some key, apply an aggregate or transformation to each group, then combine the results. For example, to sum balances by product: `df.groupby('ProductType')['Balance'].sum()`. This yields a Series (index=ProductType, values=Sum).

TEC-20.title: pandas Merge/Join vs SQL Join
TEC-20.one_screen: Pandas `merge` function performs SQL-like joins. For example, `pd.merge(df1, df2, on='key', how='inner')` is analogous to `SELECT * FROM df1 JOIN df2 ON df1.key=df2.key`. The `how` parameter can be `'inner'`, `'left'`, `'right'`, or `'outer'`, just like SQL joins. When merging, common columns (keys) must match on name or be specified via `left_on`/`right_on`. After merge, index labels are reset unless you preserve them.

TEC-21.title: Handling Missing Data in pandas
TEC-21.one_screen: Pandas represents missing data as `NaN` (for floats) or `NaT` (for datetimes) or `None` in object columns. Use `df.isna()` (or `isnull()`) to detect missing values, returning a boolean mask. You can drop rows or columns with missing data via `df.dropna()`, or fill values with `df.fillna(value)`. For example, `df['Balance'].fillna(0, inplace=True)` replaces missing balances with 0.

TEC-22.title: Dates and Time Series Indexing in pandas
TEC-22.one_screen: Pandas has robust datetime support. Convert columns to datetime with `pd.to_datetime()`, then you can use date methods. A `DatetimeIndex` (when you set a datetime column as the index) enables time-based indexing and resampling. To generate regular time sequences, `pd.date_range(start, end, freq='M')` creates a monthly-end index. You can then align or reindex data by time, and use `df.resample('M').sum()` to aggregate by month.

TEC-24.title: Code Quality: Reproducibility, Testing, Version Control
TEC-24.one_screen: Treat analytical scripts like software. Use virtual environments (`venv`/`conda`) and a `requirements.txt` to pin library versions, ensuring others can reproduce the environment. For example, `pip freeze > requirements.txt` captures exact package versions. Use clear folder structure and document data sources in code comments.
