TLM-01.title: What a bank treasury actually does
TLM-01.one_screen: Bank treasury is the balance-sheet control centre that converts customer activity into managed funding, liquidity, interest-rate and market positions. Unlike a corporate treasury, it does not merely finance an operating business: maturity transformation and financial intermediation are themselves part of the bank’s business model.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10
Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016

TLM-02.title: Banking book versus trading book
TLM-02.one_screen: The banking-book/trading-book boundary is not shorthand for “held long term” versus “traded frequently”; it is a regulatory classification determining which risk framework applies. Moving an exposure across that boundary can change valuation, capital treatment, risk measurement, governance and permissible hedging recognition.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V
European Banking Authority, *Guidelines on IRRBB and CSRBB*, EBA/GL/2022/14

TLM-03.title: The balance sheet as a set of mismatches
TLM-03.one_screen: ALM begins by discarding accounting labels and viewing the balance sheet as dated cash flows and repricing events. Risk appears because the timing, rate basis, optionality and liquidity characteristics of assets do not line up perfectly with those of liabilities.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98

TLM-04.title: Where IRRBB comes from
TLM-04.one_screen: IRRBB is not one risk but four interacting mechanisms: repricing gap, yield-curve shape, basis and optionality. A balance sheet can appear matched against one mechanism and remain materially exposed to another.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V

TLM-05.title: Economic value of equity versus net interest income
TLM-05.one_screen: EVE asks how interest-rate shocks change the present value of the banking book; NII asks how they change near-term interest earnings and expense. Neither dominates the other because they expose different parts of the same balance-sheet risk.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V paragraphs 46–50 and 84–89

TLM-06.title: Duration and its limits
TLM-06.one_screen: Duration compresses a stream of cash flows into an approximate first-order sensitivity to interest rates. It is powerful for intuition and dangerous when treated as a complete model of a bank balance sheet.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V

TLM-07.title: Gap analysis and repricing buckets
TLM-07.one_screen: Repricing gap analysis places rate-sensitive assets and liabilities into the periods when they next reprice, then compares the two sides. It is a map of timing mismatch, not a complete forecast of earnings or value.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V

TLM-08.title: Behavioural modelling of non-maturity deposits
TLM-08.one_screen: A non-maturity deposit has an overnight contractual withdrawal right but may behave like multi-year funding. ALM therefore models both how long balances remain and how their administered rates respond to market rates; those assumptions can dominate measured IRRBB.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V
European Banking Authority, *Guidelines on IRRBB and CSRBB*, EBA/GL/2022/14
Federal Reserve, *Interest Rate Risk: Interagency Advisory*, January 2010

TLM-09.title: Prepayment, early redemption and pipeline risk
TLM-09.one_screen: Customer and business options make future banking-book cash flows conditional rather than fixed. Prepayments shorten assets, early withdrawals shorten liabilities, and pipeline commitments can create exposure before an instrument has even reached the balance sheet.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V

TLM-10.title: IRRBB stress tests and supervisory outliers
TLM-10.one_screen: An IRRBB stress test asks whether the balance sheet remains tolerable under severe rate paths and stressed customer behaviour; a supervisory outlier test is a regulatory screening device, not the bank’s complete risk appetite. Passing the outlier test does not prove IRRBB is safe.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP31
Reserve Bank of India, *Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Forthcoming Instructions) Directions, 2025*, Chapter V paragraphs 78–89
European Banking Authority, *Regulatory Technical Standards on IRRBB supervisory outlier tests*, 2024
Federal Reserve, *Interest Rate Risk: Interagency Advisory*, January 2010

TLM-11.title: Hedging IRRBB and hedge accounting
TLM-11.one_screen: An economic hedge changes the bank’s risk; hedge accounting changes how qualifying hedge effects appear in financial statements. A hedge can be economically effective without receiving hedge-accounting treatment, and accounting treatment must never determine whether the underlying risk is actually controlled.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, *Deferral of Implementation of Indian Accounting Standards (Ind AS)*, RBI/2018-2019/146, DBR.BP.BC.No.29/21.07.001/2018-19
Reserve Bank of India, *Implementation of Indian Accounting Standards — NBFCs and ARCs*, DOR (NBFC) circular, 13 March 2020
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98

TLM-12.title: Funding liquidity risk versus market liquidity risk
TLM-12.one_screen: Funding liquidity risk is the risk that the bank cannot obtain cash when obligations fall due without unacceptable loss; market liquidity risk is the risk that an asset cannot be sold or financed quickly near its expected value. One can trigger the other, but they are not the same risk.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *High-quality liquid assets*, Basel Framework LCR30

TLM-13.title: High-quality liquid assets
TLM-13.one_screen: HQLA are not simply “safe securities”; they are assets that the liquidity framework recognises as capable of generating cash rapidly under stress with little loss. Eligibility, operational availability, encumbrance, haircut and portfolio composition all matter.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *High-quality liquid assets*, Basel Framework LCR30
Reserve Bank of India, *Basel III Framework on Liquidity Standards – LCR*, RBI/2022-23/25, DOR.LRG.REC.19/21.04.098/2022-23
Reserve Bank of India, *LCR – Review of Haircuts on HQLA and Run-off Rates*, RBI/2025-26/27, DOR.LRG.REC.18/03.10.001/2025-26
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Applicability Thresholds for Regulatory Capital and Liquidity Requirements*, Bulletin 2019-52

TLM-14.title: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio
TLM-14.one_screen: LCR asks whether a bank has enough recognised HQLA to withstand modelled net cash outflows over a severe 30-calendar-day stress period. It is a standardised short-horizon resilience test, not a forecast of the bank’s actual next 30 days.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Calculation of the LCR*, Basel Framework LCR20
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *High-quality liquid assets*, Basel Framework LCR30
Reserve Bank of India, *LCR – Review of Haircuts on HQLA and Run-off Rates*, RBI/2025-26/27, DOR.LRG.REC.18/03.10.001/2025-26
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, *Applicability Thresholds for Regulatory Capital and Liquidity Requirements*, Bulletin 2019-52

TLM-15.title: The Net Stable Funding Ratio
TLM-15.one_screen: NSFR asks whether the bank’s longer-term assets and activities are supported by sufficiently stable funding over a one-year structural horizon. Where LCR is a short-term stress-buffer test, NSFR is a balance-sheet funding-structure test.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Net Stable Funding Ratio*, Basel Framework NSF30
Financial Stability Institute, *Net Stable Funding Ratio — Executive Summary*

Federal Reserve, *Agencies issue final rule to strengthen resilience of large banks*, 20 October 2020

TLM-16.title: Intraday liquidity
TLM-16.one_screen: A bank can end the day liquid and still fail during the day if payments arrive before offsetting receipts. Intraday liquidity is the capacity to meet payment and settlement obligations at the required time, not merely by the reporting cut-off.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Monitoring tools for intraday liquidity management*, BCBS 248
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144

TLM-17.title: Survival horizon and liquidity stress testing
TLM-17.one_screen: Liquidity stress testing converts a scenario into daily cash needs and monetisable resources; survival horizon is the time until the bank can no longer meet obligations under that scenario without prohibited or extraordinary assumptions. Unlike LCR, it is institution-specific and can span multiple phases of stress.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Liquidity risk monitoring metrics*, Basel Framework SRP50

TLM-18.title: Contingency funding plans
TLM-18.one_screen: A contingency funding plan converts liquidity stress analysis into an executable crisis playbook: triggers, decision rights, funding actions, collateral, communications and escalation. A list of theoretical funding sources is not a CFP unless those sources can actually be mobilised under stress.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Federal Reserve, *12 CFR 252.34 — Liquidity Risk-Management Requirements*

TLM-19.title: ILAAP and the naming trap
TLM-19.one_screen: ILAAP is the formal internal liquidity adequacy assessment terminology used in UK and EU supervisory architecture; it is not the universal global name for bank liquidity assessment. India and the US require liquidity-risk governance, stress testing and contingency planning through their own frameworks without universally relabelling that architecture “ILAAP”.

sources.label: Prudential Regulation Authority, *The PRA’s approach to supervising liquidity and funding risks*, SS24/15, January 2026

Federal Reserve, *12 CFR 252.34 — Liquidity Risk-Management Requirements*

TLM-20.title: What funds transfer pricing solves
TLM-20.one_screen: FTP gives each business an internal price for the funding and liquidity consequences it creates, separating customer-product performance from centrally managed balance-sheet risk. Without FTP, business profitability can look strongest precisely where the bank is taking the most hidden maturity and liquidity risk.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016
Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144

TLM-21.title: Matched-maturity FTP
TLM-21.one_screen: Matched-maturity FTP prices each asset or liability against internal funding of a comparable effective tenor rather than against one pooled average funding rate. It removes the accidental subsidy that otherwise makes long-dated assets look as cheap to fund as short-dated ones.

sources.label: Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10
Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016

TLM-22.title: The FTP curve and its components
TLM-22.one_screen: An FTP curve converts tenor into the bank’s internal marginal value or cost of funding; it normally combines a reference-rate component with institution-specific term-liquidity economics, while contingent liquidity costs are allocated to exposures that can create stressed funding needs. The components must remain interpretable or business behaviour cannot be controlled.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016
Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10

TLM-23.title: Charging liquidity to the business that consumes it
TLM-23.one_screen: Liquidity cost belongs with the activity that creates the need to fund or hold a buffer, even when treasury centrally executes the funding. Central execution without decentralised pricing hides the risk from the business decision that created it.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144

TLM-24.title: FTP for non-maturity deposits
TLM-24.one_screen: NMD FTP is difficult because the product has no contractual term from which to select a transfer rate. The transfer credit must be built from a governed behavioural replication of stable balances and repricing behaviour, not from either overnight maturity or an arbitrary long-term tenor.

sources.label: Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10
Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Application guidance on interest rate risk in the banking book*, Basel Framework SRP98

TLM-25.title: How bad FTP distorts behaviour
TLM-25.one_screen: FTP is a behavioural control disguised as an internal price. Set it wrongly and rational business lines will optimise the wrong objective—creating excessive maturity transformation, unstable funding, cheap commitments or artificial deposit growth while reported product profitability still looks attractive.

sources.label: Federal Reserve, *Interagency Guidance on Funds Transfer Pricing Related to Funding and Contingent Liquidity Risks*, March 2016
Financial Stability Institute, *Liquidity transfer pricing: a guide to better practice*, FSI Occasional Paper No. 10

TLM-26.title: Why a solvent bank can fail
TLM-26.one_screen: Solvency is about whether assets ultimately cover liabilities with adequate capital; liquidity is about whether cash is available when payment is due. A bank can possess positive economic net worth yet fail if it cannot monetise assets or obtain funding fast enough to settle immediate obligations.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *High-quality liquid assets*, Basel Framework LCR30

TLM-27.title: The credit-liquidity feedback loop
TLM-27.one_screen: Credit deterioration can create liquidity stress, and liquidity stress can create additional credit losses; the loop runs through collateral, funding confidence, asset sales and customer drawdowns. Stress models that shock credit and liquidity independently can therefore miss the mechanism that makes combined crises severe.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, *Principles for Sound Liquidity Risk Management and Supervision*, BCBS 144
Federal Reserve, *12 CFR 252.34 — Liquidity Risk-Management Requirements*

TLM-28.title: India’s SLR, MSF, FALLCR and LCR interaction
TLM-28.one_screen: India’s distinctive feature is that specified government securities held within the mandatory SLR can also receive LCR HQLA recognition through the MSF and FALLCR carve-outs. SLR and LCR are different requirements, but RBI deliberately permits overlap so qualifying statutory holdings can provide recognised stress liquidity.

sources.label: Reserve Bank of India, *Basel III Framework on Liquidity Standards – LCR*, RBI/2022-23/25, DOR.LRG.REC.19/21.04.098/2022-23

TLM-29.title: Cross-jurisdiction liquidity and IRRBB architecture
TLM-29.one_screen: Basel supplies the common LCR, NSFR and IRRBB architecture, but national implementation is not identical: India has the SLR/FALLCR overlay and a forthcoming 2025 IRRBB regime; the UK embeds liquidity adequacy in PRA ILAAP supervision; the EU combines CRR liquidity ratios with EBA IRRBB/CSRBB standards; the US tailors LCR/NSFR by firm category and uses liquidity-risk/CFP terminology rather than a universal ILAAP label.

TLM-30.title: The integrated ALM decision cycle
TLM-30.one_screen: ALM is the repeated process of converting the balance sheet into risk measures, comparing them with appetite and constraints, changing pricing, funding or hedges, and then measuring again. The decisive skill is understanding that capital, liquidity, IRRBB and FTP are different views of one evolving balance sheet rather than separate regulatory exercises.

TRD-01.title: Equities
TRD-01.one_screen: An equity is a residual claim on a company: debt and other senior claims are paid first, and shareholders own what remains. Its price therefore reflects both expected future cash generation and the uncertainty around that residual.

sources.label: U.S. SEC, Investor.gov, Stocks

TRD-02.title: Fixed Income
TRD-02.one_screen: A fixed-income instrument converts financing into contractual cash flows: interest, principal and sometimes embedded options. Its value is driven by the timing and certainty of those cash flows and the discount rates used to value them.

sources.label: U.S. SEC, Investor.gov, What Are Corporate Bonds?

TRD-03.title: Clean Price and Dirty Price
TRD-03.one_screen: A bond quote may exclude accrued interest even though settlement does not. Clean price is the quoted price without accrued interest; dirty price is the amount economically paid for the bond before fees: clean price plus accrued interest.

sources.label: FINRA, Understanding Bond Yield and Return

TRD-04.title: Yield to Maturity and the Price–Yield Relationship
TRD-04.one_screen: Yield to maturity is the single discount rate that equates a bond’s market price with the present value of its promised remaining cash flows. For a plain fixed-rate bond, price and yield move in opposite directions because a higher discount rate lowers present value.

sources.label: FINRA, Understanding Bond Yield and Return
U.S. SEC, Investor Bulletin: Fixed Income Investments — When Interest Rates Go Up, Prices of Fixed-Rate Bonds Fall

TRD-05.title: Duration and Convexity
TRD-05.one_screen: Duration is the first-order estimate of how a bond price changes when yield changes; convexity is the second-order correction for the curve in the price–yield relationship. Duration gives the slope, convexity improves the estimate when moves are larger.

sources.label: FINRA, Brush Up on Bonds: Interest Rate Changes and Duration

TRD-06.title: Credit Spreads
TRD-06.one_screen: A credit spread is the extra yield demanded over a reference curve for bearing risks not present in the reference instrument. It is compensation for expected credit loss plus risk, liquidity and technical premia—not a direct default-probability reading.

sources.label: FINRA, Spread the Word: What You Need to Know About Bond Spreads

TRD-07.title: The Yield Curve
TRD-07.one_screen: A yield curve maps interest rates or yields across maturities for instruments sharing a defined credit and market basis. Level, slope and curvature are separate sources of risk: the curve can move without shifting in parallel.

sources.label: FINRA, Understanding Bond Yield and Return

TRD-08.title: Repo and Reverse Repo
TRD-08.one_screen: A repo is economically secured borrowing: one party sells securities now and agrees to repurchase equivalent securities later at a higher price. The same transaction is a reverse repo from the cash lender’s perspective.

sources.label: ICMA, Repo and Collateral Markets

TRD-09.title: Securities Lending
TRD-09.one_screen: Securities lending temporarily transfers securities to a borrower against collateral, with an obligation to return equivalent securities. The lender earns a fee or investment spread; the borrower obtains the securities, often to support short selling, settlement or market making.

sources.label: ISLA, Guidance Notes to the Global Master Securities Lending Agreement (2010 Version)

TRD-10.title: FX Spot, Forward and Swap
TRD-10.one_screen: FX spot exchanges two currencies near the trade date; an FX forward locks an exchange for a future date; an FX swap combines a spot leg and an offsetting forward leg. The key is to track both currencies, both directions and every value date.

sources.label: BIS, Dollar debt in FX swaps and forwards: huge, missing and growing
RBI, Foreign Exchange (Forex) Transactions FAQs
BIS, Uncovering FX settlement risk: new measures from the 2025 BIS Triennial Survey

TRD-11.title: Covered Interest Parity and Forward Points
TRD-11.one_screen: Covered interest parity links spot FX, forward FX and interest rates in two currencies under no-arbitrage. Forward points are therefore primarily a funding relationship, not a directional prediction—and persistent basis can appear when balance sheet and hedging constraints make arbitrage costly.

sources.label: BIS, Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis
BIS, Covered interest parity: a forecasting approach to estimate the neutral band

TRD-12.title: Non-Deliverable Forwards
TRD-12.one_screen: An NDF locks an exchange-rate outcome without exchanging the restricted underlying currency at maturity. The parties cash-settle the difference between the contracted forward rate and an agreed fixing, usually in a freely deliverable settlement currency.

sources.label: BIS, Non-deliverable forwards: impact of currency internationalisation and derivatives reform
RBI, Master Direction — Risk Management and Inter-Bank Dealings

TRD-13.title: Derivatives: Linear and Non-Linear Payoffs
TRD-13.one_screen: A derivative takes its value from an underlying market variable. Linear derivatives change value roughly one-for-one with that variable; non-linear derivatives change sensitivity as the underlying moves, which is why options require more than a single directional risk measure.

sources.label: BIS, OTC derivatives statistics explanatory notes

TRD-14.title: Forwards and Futures
TRD-14.one_screen: Forwards and futures both lock future economic exposure, but the market infrastructure differs. A forward is typically bilateral and customisable; a future is standardised, exchange-traded and margined through a clearing framework.

sources.label: CFTC, Futures Glossary

TRD-15.title: Options: Moneyness, Intrinsic Value and Time Value
TRD-15.one_screen: An option buys asymmetry: the holder has a right, not an obligation, to transact at the strike. Option premium is commonly decomposed into intrinsic value plus time value, while moneyness describes where spot sits relative to strike.

sources.label: CME Group, Options Analytics: Greeks and Implied Volatility

TRD-16.title: The Option Greeks
TRD-16.one_screen: The Greeks are local sensitivities, not separate risks: delta measures underlying-price sensitivity, gamma the change in delta, vega volatility sensitivity and theta time decay. They describe how an option’s value responds when one input moves while others are held approximately constant.

sources.label: CME Group, Options Analytics: Greeks and Implied Volatility
CME Group, Options Vega — The Greeks

TRD-17.title: Optionality
TRD-17.one_screen: Optionality means one party controls a future choice whose value changes with market conditions. It can be explicit, as in an option contract, or embedded inside another product, as in a callable bond or prepayable loan.

sources.label: FINRA, Brush Up on Bonds: Interest Rate Changes and Duration
CME Group, Options Analytics: Greeks and Implied Volatility

TRD-18.title: Interest Rate Swaps
TRD-18.one_screen: A plain interest-rate swap exchanges fixed and floating interest cash flows on a notional principal. The notional usually is not exchanged; the swap converts the economic rate exposure of an asset or liability without refinancing the underlying principal.

sources.label: ISDA, 2021 ISDA Interest Rate Derivatives Definitions

TRD-19.title: IBOR Reform and Risk-Free Rates
TRD-19.one_screen: LIBOR is over. Modern rate markets use alternative overnight risk-free or near-risk-free benchmarks and explicit fallback mechanics. The durable lesson is that replacing a term unsecured bank rate with an overnight rate changes conventions, not just the ticker.

sources.label: FCA, About LIBOR transition
FCA, The end of LIBOR
ISDA, 2021 Interest Rate Derivatives Definitions InfoHub

TRD-20.title: OIS and Discounting
TRD-20.one_screen: An overnight index swap exchanges a fixed rate against an overnight-rate-based floating leg. In collateralised derivatives, overnight-rate curves became central to discounting because the collateral remuneration rate is part of the economics of funding future cash flows.

sources.label: ISDA, 2021 ISDA Interest Rate Derivatives Definitions

TRD-21.title: Credit Default Swaps
TRD-21.one_screen: A CDS transfers defined credit-event risk on a reference entity or obligation. The protection buyer pays premium; the protection seller makes a credit-event settlement if the contractually defined event occurs.

sources.label: ISDA, Credit Derivatives

TRD-22.title: Credit Indices
TRD-22.one_screen: A credit index packages CDS exposure to a standard basket of reference entities into one tradable contract. It gives broad credit-spread exposure, while single-name defaults are handled through defined index mechanics rather than turning the product into a static bond fund.

sources.label: ISDA, Credit Derivatives

TRD-23.title: Exchange-Traded and OTC Markets
TRD-23.one_screen: Exchange trading standardises the contract and market process; OTC trading allows bilateral or platform-based negotiation of bespoke terms. Trading venue, clearing venue and legal counterparty are separate questions.

sources.label: BIS CPMI-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures

TRD-24.title: Central Counterparties and Novation
TRD-24.one_screen: A CCP interposes itself between market participants so each faces the CCP rather than the original trading counterparty for cleared obligations. Novation changes the legal counterparty; it does not make risk disappear.

sources.label: BIS CPMI-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures
BIS CPMI, Recommendations for Central Counterparties

TRD-25.title: Clearing, Settlement and Settlement Cycles
TRD-25.one_screen: Clearing determines what each party owes; settlement discharges those obligations by moving cash and securities. T+1 means standard settlement is one business day after trade date—it does not mean every market, instrument or failed trade settles then.

sources.label: SEBI, Introduction of Beta version of T+0 rolling settlement cycle on optional basis in addition to the existing T+1 settlement cycle in Equity Cash Markets
SEBI, Enhancement in the scope of optional T+0 rolling settlement cycle
U.S. SEC, SEC Chair Gensler Statement on Upcoming Implementation of T+1 Settlement Cycle
UK HM Treasury, Accelerated Settlement (T+1)
European Commission, T+1 settlement

TRD-26.title: The Trade Lifecycle
TRD-26.one_screen: A trade is not complete when it is executed. It must be captured, enriched, validated, confirmed, cleared where relevant, settled, valued, margined, reported and maintained through every lifecycle event until maturity or close-out.

sources.label: BIS CPMI-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures
ISDA, Common Domain Model

TRD-27.title: Front Office, Middle Office and Back Office
TRD-27.one_screen: Front, middle and back office are responsibility patterns, not universal organisation charts. Front office takes and manages commercial risk; middle-office functions control and explain it; back office completes confirmations, payments, settlements and records.

sources.label: BCBS, Corporate governance principles for banks

TRD-28.title: Static Data and Reference Data
TRD-28.one_screen: Reference data tells systems what an entity, instrument, calendar or code means; transactional data tells them what happened. A wrong static field can contaminate thousands of correct trades, which is why golden sources, effective dating and lineage matter.

sources.label: GLEIF, Introducing the Legal Entity Identifier
ISO, International Securities Identification Number (ISIN)

TRD-29.title: The Derivatives Documentation Stack
TRD-29.one_screen: Derivative documentation is layered: a master agreement sets relationship-wide legal rules, schedules customise them, credit-support documents govern collateral and confirmations define individual transactions. The economic trade cannot be understood safely from the confirmation alone.

sources.label: ISDA, 2002 ISDA Master Agreement
ISDA, 2021 ISDA Interest Rate Derivatives Definitions
ICMA, Repo and Collateral Markets
ISLA, Guidance Notes to the GMSLA 2010

TRD-30.title: ISDA Master Agreement and Close-Out Netting
TRD-30.one_screen: The ISDA Master Agreement turns many OTC derivatives into one governed relationship. If termination is triggered, close-out netting values the covered terminated transactions and collapses them into a single net amount, subject to the agreement and applicable law.

sources.label: ISDA, 2002 ISDA Master Agreement
ISDA, ISDA Close-out Framework
ISDA, Collateral Market Review

TRD-31.title: Credit Support Annex and Collateral
TRD-31.one_screen: A CSA governs collateral for a derivatives relationship. It converts changing mark-to-market exposure into collateral calls according to agreed thresholds, eligible assets, valuation rules and transfer mechanics; it changes counterparty and liquidity risk, not the underlying derivative payoff.

sources.label: ISDA, Collateral Market Review
ISDA, ISDA Close-out Framework

TRD-32.title: Banking Book versus Trading Book
TRD-32.one_screen: The regulatory book boundary determines which capital framework applies to an instrument. Trading intent matters, but modern Basel rules add mandatory classifications, presumptions, documentation and tight restrictions on switching so that banks cannot move positions simply to obtain lower capital.

sources.label: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Basel Framework RBC25 — Boundary between the banking book and the trading book
Reserve Bank of India, Master Direction — Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio of Commercial Banks (Directions), 2023
Bank of England/PRA, PS1/26 — Implementation of Basel 3.1: Final rules

Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Bulletin 2026-9
